objects.title: Ayam-Ayam Bernaga
objects.caption:
Ayam-ayam bernaga — literally "roosters and dragons" — is a traditional wedding accessory worn by brides in the Brunei Malay community. Placed above the bride's head, it is worn during the powdering night, a ceremony in which the bride and groom are separately blessed with colourful powders at their respective homes. Made in gold tones, it originated among the Malays of Kampong Ayer (the Water Village), before becoming widely used among Malay communities throughout the country.

The pairing of rooster and dragon on a bridal headpiece is deliberate. Positioned at the crown of the bride during a moment of transition, these animals serve as auspicious guardians for the beginning of married life. The rooster is associated with courage, vigilance, and the arrival of a new day through its dawn call, while the dragon carries associations of power, protection, and authority drawn from wider Asian traditions. Together, they express qualities desired for the bride’s new household: vitality, strength, and continued prosperity.

The Ayam-ayam bernaga reflects the layered symbolic world of Brunei Malay ceremonial culture, where local customs incorporated animal imagery shaped by centuries of interaction across maritime Southeast Asia. Worn at the threshold between maidenhood and marriage, the headpiece demonstrates how communities across the region transformed both familiar and mythical animals into protectors, blessings, and markers of social identity.

objects.title: Bronze Cock Standing on the Coop
objects.title_raw: Bronze Cock Standing on the Coop
objects.caption:
This bronze sculpture of a rooster, discovered at the Ban Don Ta Phet archaeological site in Kanchanaburi Province, dates to the late prehistoric period. The bird is carefully rendered with the characteristic features of a mature male chicken, including a prominent comb, hackles, long tail feathers, and sharp spurs. It stands on a bronze post that fits precisely into a bronze enclosure discovered nearby during archeological excavations, suggesting that the two objects originally formed part of a single composition. Excavations also revealed traces of hemp textile adhering to the rooster’s tail feathers, possibly from a burial wrapping or garments placed with the deceased.

The object demonstrates the advanced metalworking skills of the Ban Don Ta Phet community. Analysis shows that the bronze contains approximately 23-28 percent tin, producing a distinctive golden-silver appearance and reflecting the same casting knowledge found in other bronze objects from the site. Its production required specialised knowledge of alloy composition, mould-making, and metal casting, placing it among the community’s more technically accomplished objects.

Its archaeological context also reveals the wider connections of this prehistoric society. The bronze rooster and enclosure were found alongside rich burial assemblages containing glass beads, carnelian, agate ornaments, silk fragments, and Manila hemp fibres, indicating contact with communities across long-distance exchange networks. The presence of woven hemp textiles further demonstrates the sophisticated use of natural fibres alongside metal technology during this period.

The rooster also provides evidence of the close relationship between humans and chickens in prehistoric Thailand. Chicken remains have been found at several Neolithic and Bronze Age sites, including Ban Chiang and Ban Non Wat, indicating that domesticated chickens were already part of community life. This bronze representation transforms that familiar animal into a carefully crafted object associated with burial and remembrance.

Together, the rooster sculpture and its burial context reveal how an animal embedded in everyday life could also enter ritual worlds. Through bronze, textile, and burial practice, the chicken became part of a larger expression of identity and craftsmanship among prehistoric communities of mainland Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Domestic Chicken
objects.caption:
The chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) that many of us are familiar with is a domesticated form of the red junglefowl (Gallus gallus) which is native to Southeast Asia and parts of South Asia. While the domestic chicken can be found with a variety of plumage colours and forms, the red junglefowl has several distinct physical characteristics. The adult male rooster has a red comb, facial skin and lappets, white ear patches, golden-yellow neck feathers, maroon scapulars and an arched dark green tail. In contrast, the female hen is less flamboyant with a drab brown plumage and golden neck feathers.

Archaeological evidence supports the presence of domestic chickens in Southeast Asia before 6000 BC, and researchers have suggested that this bird was also brought to China and India within the next 3000-4000 years. With such a long history of presence within human societies, the chicken has also become deeply embedded in many cultures in various ways. The cock is associated with courage and perseverance in East Timor, while in several regional religions it is a sacred creature used in worship and  rituals.

The domesticated chicken has also been deeply entwined in the practice of cockfighting. This sport has a long global history and holds particular cultural importance within the Philippines and Indonesia. In Bali, ceremonial cockfighting (known as tabuh rah, the 'spilling of blood') is a temple practice intended to provide an offering to the spirits.

objects.title: Lawi Ayam Cock-Feather Dagger (Southern Dagger / Cock-Spur Knife)
objects.title_raw: Lawi Ayam Cock-Feather Dagger  (Southern Dagger / Cock-Spur Knife)
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
The Lawi Ayam, which translates literally to "the tail feather of a mature rooster", is a traditional close-quarters weapon whose name determines its form: the blade's gracefully curved, slender profile replicates the sweep of a rooster's tail feather, an analogy that shaped every decision in its construction. This example comes from the Patani School of Bladesmithing (Sakon Chang Pattani), one of the most historically significant centres for weapon production in Southern Thailand.

The weapon demonstrates the high level of craftsmanship associated with Patani bladesmithing. Its hilt is carved from Mai Kaeo Dee Pli (Orange Jessamine), a prized local hardwood, into the form of a rooster’s head and fitted with a brass ferrule and protective finger guard. The blade was forged through pattern-welding, layering iron and carbon steel through repeated folding and hammering to create the patterned surface known as Lai Mai Phok, a regional expression of the pamor tradition found across Malay and Indonesian blades. Its sheath, made from Hill Neem wood with an ebony inlay, further reflects the careful selection of materials associated with both craftsmanship and auspicious qualities.

The Lawi Ayam was carried widely across Pattani, Songkhla, Phatthalung, Trang, and the northern Malay sultanates. Unlike large battlefield weapons, its compact size allowed it to be worn discreetly within a sarong or waist belt, ready for immediate use. In close-combat traditions recorded in Malay martial texts such as the Kitab Silat, its inward-curving blade was suited for hooking and controlling an opponent’s movements, reflecting a fighting style built around speed, precision, and adaptability.

The rooster form gave the weapon meanings beyond its practical function. Across Southern Thai and Malay communities, the rooster was associated with courage, vigilance, and fighting spirit. As the bird that announces dawn and drives away darkness, it was understood as a symbol of alertness and protection. By shaping the weapon after the rooster’s tail feather, makers and owners connected the qualities of the animal with those expected of the bearer: bravery, agility, and resilience.

The Lawi Ayam reflects a shared martial and symbolic tradition that developed across the historical landscape of Southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula. Its form preserves both the technical knowledge of Patani bladesmiths and a wider regional understanding of the rooster as a symbol of strength and protection.

objects.title: Rooster-Headed Brass Charcoal Iron adorned with Dragon and Phoenix Reliefs
objects.title_raw: Rooster-Headed Brass Charcoal Iron adorned with  Dragon and Phoenix Reliefs
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This rooster-headed brass charcoal iron is cast from thick, high-density brass alloy. Its form resembles a pointed hull or a maritime sailing galleon. This shape was engineered to provide substantial gravitational weight, allowing the user to smooth heavy fabric fibers with minimal physical exertion. The hollow interior houses a chamber for burning charcoal, with an internal baffle plate distributing thermal energy uniformly across the soleplate. Along the lateral walls, a series of draft vents allow oxygen to circulate and keep the embers burning evenly. Larger models featuring nine air vents are known locally as "Nine-Hole Irons" (Tao Rit Kao Ru).

The defining mechanical feature of this iron is the sculpted rooster head (Hua Kai) cast as a functional latch at the front apex. This component securely locks the hinged lid during operation, preventing red-hot embers or fine ash from spilling out and ruining the textiles. This unique feature gave rise to its colloquial regional name, the "Rooster-Headed Iron" (Tao Rit Hua Kai).

Operating the iron required empirical knowledge refined through practice. The user filled the core with lit charcoal, fanned it to draw air through the vents, and rubbed the hot brass soleplate over a fresh green banana leaf before pressing. The natural wax released from the heated leaf created a smooth, non-stick surface that protected delicate fabrics while leaving a faint fragrance on the cloth.

The iron's exterior is engraved with low-relief depictions of the dragon (Mangkon) and phoenix (Hong). Within Chinese cosmology, these creatures form an auspicious pairing: the dragon representing supreme authority and the masculine forces of heaven; the phoenix, virtue, grace, and feminine power. Together they signify marital harmony and domestic abundance, qualities fitting for an object used to prepare clothing for weddings, festivals, and communal ceremonies. The rooster, meanwhile, represents the household virtues of tireless diligence, early rising, and spiritual alertness. Their combination on a domestic iron reflects the historic settlement of Overseas Chinese communities in trading hubs along the Malay Peninsula, in Nakhon Si Thammarat, Songkhla, and Phuket, where such objects were either imported from maritime foundries in southern China or produced locally by Chinese-diaspora metalsmiths. As such, this iron is a demonstration of how communities across maritime Southeast Asia adapted imported technologies by giving them meanings rooted in their own cultural landscapes

objects.title: Sulang
objects.caption:
The Sulang is a traditional storage box made of copper. This item was commonly used to hold water during gatherings such as weddings and thanksgiving events. It was also used to store rice and other dry foods. While this specimen is now preserved by the Museums Department, similar Sulangs continue to be kept as decorative objects in some Bruneian homes.

The handles of this vessel invite close attention. At first glance they may suggest a buffalo, but taken as a whole — the legs, the overall form, and particularly the flowing tail — the form is more readily read as a bird. Most likely, it depicts either a Rhinoceros Hornbill (Buceros rhinoceros) or a rooster (Gallus gallus), both of which are common in Brunei Darussalam. The hornbill, native to Borneo and deeply embedded in the spiritual and decorative life of the island's communities, carries associations of protection, vitality, and sacred guardianship that make it a natural presence on a vessel holding the staples of food and water on important occasions. Meanwhile, the rooster carries its own distinct cultural weight. Prized as a competitive animal in traditional cockfighting (Sabung Ayam), the winning rooster was a source of considerable pride for the community. The bird's associations with fortune, energy, and domestic abundance gave it a prominent place in the material culture of everyday life.

The uncertainty surrounding the bird’s identity reflects the flexibility of Brunei’s folk craft traditions, where animal forms were not always fixed representations but carried overlapping associations drawn from the surrounding environment and cultural life. Whether intended as a hornbill or a rooster, the motif reveals a wider Southeast Asian tradition of embedding the qualities of animals — protection, vitality, and prosperity — within the objects of everyday use.

objects.title: Tempayan , Large Earthen Storage Jars
objects.caption:
These large earthenware storage jars likely produced in southern China or Southeast Asia between the late 18th and early 20th century, were household staples in Peranakan Chinese homes across maritime Southeast Asia. Crafted from high-fired clay, they features hand-painted ochre and brown decorative motifs including birds in flight, floral scrolls, and bamboo-inspired designs. These motifs drew from Chinese visual traditions in which plants and animals conveyed wishes for harmony, prosperity, longevity, and abundance. Such jars were used for storing water, grains, pickled vegetables, and other household provisions.

In Peranakan households, the tempayan occupied a central place in daily life not only because of its practical function, but also because of the meanings attached to its decoration. Everyday objects were often transformed through auspicious imagery, allowing domestic spaces to express cultural identity and aspirations. The birds painted on this jar, including chickens, belong to this tradition of embedding the natural world into household objects. The rooster, associated across Chinese and Southeast Asian communities with diligence, vitality, and the arrival of dawn, brought these qualities into the sphere of everyday provision and family life.

These similar tempayan were found at the Baba & Nyonya Heritage Museum, Melaka, and the National Museum Bangkok, reflecting shared domestic practices across the region. Bird motifs, often depicted on the jars, were included for auspicious meanings. Most tempayan were produced in China and widely exported across Asia. Larger jars were commonly used for water storage, while smaller ones held pickles, rice, or other dry ingredients.

By placing such imagery on a vessel used to preserve the household’s necessities, the jar connected ordinary acts of storage and sustenance with broader hopes for prosperity and continuity, and reflects how animal symbolism woven into the material culture of everyday life across maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Tin Ingots in the Shape of Chicken
objects.title_raw: Tin Ingots in the Shape of Chicken
objects.caption:
These tin ingots, produced in animal forms including the rooster, represent a distinctive tradition of zoomorphic currency used across the Malay Peninsula and beyond. The state of Perak was the primary producer of such ingots, crafting forms including elephants, tortoises, crocodiles, goats, roosters, grasshoppers, fish, and crabs from at least the 16th century. In commerce, they served a dual function: as standard weights used to measure the accuracy of other tin blocks and traded goods, and, at times, as a direct medium of exchange.

Although their original purposes have been debated — with suggestions that some may have served as talismans, weights, or even objects of display — historical records confirm their role in monetary transactions. In the Kinta Valley of Perak during the mid-19th century, for example, a cast tin cockerel (gambar ayam) was valued at 10 pitis, or 100 duit ayam, copper tokens bearing the image of a fighting cock issued by certain Singapore merchants. The rooster was therefore not just a decorative form, but a recognisable unit of value within regional economies.

The use of animal-shaped tin ingots was not confined to Perak. Archaeological discoveries and historical records indicate similar forms in Sumatra, Southern Thailand, and the Philippines, reflecting the circulation of tin, trade practices, and monetary systems across maritime Southeast Asia. Their recurring animal forms reveal how economic exchange operated through locally familiar animals, linking commerce with the shared visual languages of communities connected by trade.

objects.title: Wooden Cold-Press Cake Molds with Elephant, Horse, and Fowl Motifs
objects.title_raw: Wooden Cold-Press Cake Molds with  Elephant, Horse, and Fowl Motifs
title_variants: Wooden Cold-Press Cake Molds with Elephant, Horse, and Fowl Motifs
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This phim yen (literally "cold mold") is a wooden pastry mold used to make Khanom Putu, a traditional pastry. Such molds are carved from durable local hardwoods such as jackfruit or velvet tamarind wood, with hollow cavities roughly 1 to 2 inches deep chiselled into detailed, recessed designs. This collection contains motifs of elephants, horses, and poultry, traditionally popular for Khanom Putu. The "cold-press" method gives the mold its name: the dough is shaped entirely inside the wooden matrix without baking or heat, then extracted with a sharp tap against a wooden table, releasing the pastry with sharp, embossed reliefs.

This heritage pastry has held an essential position within the daily life, rites of passage, and religious rituals of both Chinese and Malay-Javanese communities in Southern Thailand for centuries. It is used at births, cradle ceremonies, engagements, weddings, and circumcision rituals. During Songkran, younger generations arrange these pastries inside fine betel nut caddies or lacquerware to offer to elders in exchange for ancestral blessings. Within the Sathing Phra Peninsula, this pastry holds a profound allegorical connection to matrimony: its name sounds identical to the Thai word meaning "to hold fast" or "to intertwine," making the cake an edible prayer for marital fidelity.

Carving specific fauna onto the phim yen allowed families to embed unspoken blessings directly into the food served to guests. The Elephant (Chang) denotes absolute authority, spiritual merit, and structural prosperity — pastries stamped with this form are reserved for grand auspicious celebrations or offered to high-ranking Buddhist monks and Muslim leaders. The Horse (Ma) represents rapid progress and career advancement, standardly served at housewarmings or gifted to young adults. The Chicken (Kai), which awakens at dawn to forage, signifies industriousness, material abundance, and financial luck and is served more widely.

The phim yen tradition illustrates trans-regional interactions. Diasporic Chinese Hokkien and Baba-Peranakan communities introduced the technology of hand-carved wooden blocks for compressed pastries. They substituted Chinese mythological creatures with animals familiar to local agrarian life and folk belief: the elephant, the horse, and the chicken. Meanwhile, Malay-Javanese and Islamic traditions contributed to the pastry’s recipe.

This mold, encoding Chinese technological knowledge, Malay culinary tradition, and the symbolic vocabularies of the elephant, the horse, and the chicken, speaks to a layered process of exchange, adaptation, and sharing that shaped the Southern Thai-Malay Peninsula over centuries.

objects.title: Koffo Cloth
objects.caption:
Koffo, or hote, is a woven textile made from the fibres of the abaca banana (Musa textilis), a plant native to the Philippines that also thrives in North Sulawesi because of the region's close geographical and historical connections with the southern Philippines.

Woven primarily by women in the Sangihe and Talaud Islands, koffo cloth is valued for its strength, buoyancy, and resistance to salt water. These qualities made it well suited to maritime communities. In addition to being used as wall hangings and room dividers, abaca fibres were also made into ropes for boats and other seafaring activities.

objects.title: The Dragon Head Tortoise and Crane Ornament
objects.title_raw: The Dragon Head Tortoise and Crane Ornament
objects.caption:
This set of three brass statues features a large crane standing atop a tortoise with a dragon's head and dragon-like paws, flanked by two smaller cranes perched on tortoises with ordinary heads. These smaller pieces serve as candle holders. Together they form a composition likely displayed at an entryway, their size making a desk arrangement impractical. Their origins were not recorded by the museum, but they are believed to have been purchased or received as a gift by Mr. Chan Cheng Siew in the early 1900s, for the house that is now the Baba & Nyonya Heritage Museum.

Across Chinese, Japanese, and Korean traditions, the tortoise and crane are paired as symbols of longevity, based on the belief that both creatures possessed extraordinarily long lifespans. The tortoise represents endurance, stability, and protection, while the crane signifies peace, harmony, and purity. Together, they express the wish for a long and prosperous life.

The central figure adds another layer of auspicious meaning through its dragon-headed tortoise form. The dragon and tortoise are two of the four celestial animals in Chinese cosmology, associated respectively with power and stability. Their combination concentrates multiple forms of protection and good fortune into a single image. Within Baba and Nyonya households, the pairing of cranes and tortoises appeared widely on embroidered textiles, porcelain, jewellery, furniture, and other objects associated with status and refinement.

Crafted in durable brass, these statues were intended to endure both physically and symbolically. In this set, animals drawn from land, water, and the mythical realm were brought together to create an auspicious guardian at the threshold of the household. This set reflects how Peranakan communities adapted and preserved wider Chinese symbolic traditions within the material world of maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Tin Ingots in the Shape of Chicken
objects.title_raw: Tin Ingots in the Shape of Chicken
objects.caption:
This plaque is fashioned from thinly hammered gold, incised with the form of a turtle. Firm enough to hold its shape, it is distinct from the softer gold leaf used for gilding statues or architectural surfaces. It was discovered at Prasat Phako alongside other valuable objects, such as silver sheets, quartz, as well as gemstones carved with auspicious designs like elephants, garudas, and lotus flowers.

In Hindu belief, Vishnu, honoured as the preserver of cosmic order, descends to the mortal world in various avatars (incarnations). One of these is Kurma, the turtle, who supported Mount Mandara during the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, using his body as a pivot to provide the stability that allowed the gods to obtain the elixir of immortality. This avatar was venerated in Khmer belief, and the turtle's qualities — stillness, weight, endurance — made it the natural embodiment of divine foundation and cosmic stability.

It is with this myth that the plaque's function becomes fully legible. It  is believed to have been a votive offering placed within a foundation shrine as part of the Shilanyas ceremony, which involved the laying of the first brick to sanctify a temple structure. Prasat Phako, like other Khmer temple-towers of its period, was built as an image of Mount Meru, the cosmic axis at the centre of the Hindu-Buddhist universe. Therefore, to place the depiction of a turtle beneath a temple-mountain was to complete the cosmological picture: the turtle in the foundation, the mountain rising above, and the temple re-enacting the very act through which cosmic order was first established.

The turtle's significance, however, extends beyond the Hindu framework. As a familiar creature of the riverine ecosystems of the Mekong Delta and the broader Southeast Asian environment, its depiction equally reflects indigenous beliefs venerating animals associated with water and abundance — layers of meaning that would have coexisted with, and deepened, its Brahmanical significance.

Similar gold plaques bearing turtle forms, worked in both incision and repoussé, have been found across Southeast Asia — among them at the Óc Eo, Go Thap, and Da Noi sites of Southern Vietnam, associated with the ancient Funan kingdom (1st to 7th centuries AD) which produced some of the earliest known Hindu iconographic images in Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Traditional Maritime Boxes (Chased Hardwood Storage Caskets) in Horse and Turtle Design
objects.title_raw: Traditional Maritime Boxes (Chased Hardwood Storage Caskets)  in Horse and Turtle Design
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
Compact wooden storage chest used by communities along the Southern Thai coast for safeguarding vital provisions during deep-sea voyages. Local woodworkers selected high-density, resinous indigenous hardwoods such as Kiam wood (Cotylelobium lanceolatum) and Lumpho wood (Intsia palembanica) for their natural resistance to rot, humidity, and marine brine. The box's low-set, elongated rectangular silhouette was engineered for absolute equilibrium on the deck of a rolling vessel, preventing sliding or inversion during heavy monsoonal swells. Its lid was turned on a primitive wood lathe to ensure a hermetic friction fit, and many specimens featured tongue-and-groove slide locks or rattan tie-down cords to block sea spray. This impeccable design kept the contents of the box—tobacco, nipa palm wrapper leaves, fire-striking apparatus, currency, and family documents— bone-dry across multi-day expeditions.

What elevates the Ko-Ta into a work of folk art is its zoomorphic carving. The turtle-form casket’s domed lid, carved with stepped relief patterning mirroring the natural scutes of a marine turtle's carapace, invokes a creature that navigates thousands of miles of open ocean yet unerringly returns to shore, a talisman for the safe return the fisherman sought. Furthermore, the smooth, rounded edges of the turtle box served a practical purpose, preventing the container from snagging or tearing fragile fishing nets within the cramped spaces of the boat. Fishermen who spent their lives on water rather than land chose the horse as a spiritual companion, one that allowed the vessel to gallop across cresting ocean waves with the courage needed to survive long voyages.

Strict taboos governed the Ko-Ta onboard: under no circumstances could it be stored upside down; it had to be placed completely upright with its lid facing the heavens, a sympathetic charm ensuring stable sailing and smooth fortune. The name's Malay-Thai linguistic root, and the object's presence across Southern Thai coastal communities whose lives were shaped by the same maritime networks as the wider Malay world, reflects a shared material culture. Here practical engineering, animal symbolism, and the logic of survival at sea were inseparable.

objects.title: Zoomorphic Lime Container
objects.caption:
This glazed ceramic lime container, produced at the Phnom Dongrek kilns in Buriram Province in the 12th century, takes the form of a turtle, with a small head, rounded body with a circular opening at the centre of the back, and four small legs.It was used to hold slaked lime, an essential ingredient in betel chewing, which was mixed with betel leaf, areca nut, and other additions before consumption. Introduced to Southeast Asia through long-standing cultural connections with India, betel chewing became deeply embedded in daily life across the region, serving as both a gesture of hospitality and a shared social practice.

Although betel chewing was an everyday activity, the objects associated with it could also express identity and status. Lime containers were produced in a variety of materials, from humble everyday forms to finely crafted vessels such as this glazed ceramic example. The Phnom Dongrek kilns, located within the cultural sphere of the Khmer Empire, were known for producing sophisticated stoneware vessels in animal forms, including elephants, crocodiles, fish, and turtles, as well as figures drawn from Hindu-Buddhist traditions such as Ganesha. These forms drew simultaneously from the natural world around local communities and from wider religious and symbolic traditions.

The turtle was especially meaningful because it connected ordinary domestic practice with ideas of protection, endurance, and cosmic stability. Its hard shell was associated with safeguarding against harm, while its longevity made it an auspicious form for an object used repeatedly in daily life. Within Hindu traditions, the turtle is also associated with Vishnu’s Kurma Avatar, in which the divine tortoise supports Mount Mandara during the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, sustaining the balance of the cosmos upon its back.
By taking the form of this cosmological creature, the lime container transformed a routine household object into one carrying deeper layers of meaning. The turtle that symbolically supports the universe was brought into the everyday act of preparing betel, allowing religious imagination and domestic life to occupy the same material space.

objects.title: Greater Mousedeer
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum
objects.caption:
The Greater Mousedeer (Tragulus napu) is one of the world’s smallest hoofed mammals, a forest-dwelling creature that feeds on fallen fruits, leaf shoots, and other vegetation. Although mousedeer resemble true deer, they are distinguished by their much smaller size, slender legs, and the distinctive triangular white markings extending from the chin down the throat. Adults measure only around 50 to 60 cm from head to body. Its range follows the forested landscapes of mainland and maritime Southeast Asia, extending from Myanmar and Thailand through Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo, and Palawan in the Philippines. Although thought to have disappeared from Singapore, a population was rediscovered on Pulau Ubin in 2009. This specimen was collected in Indonesia in 1903.

Despite its small size, the mousedeer occupies an outsized place in the cultural imagination of the Malay-speaking world. Known as Sang Kancil, it is the protagonist of some of the region’s most beloved folktales. Rather than relying on strength, Sang Kancil survives through intelligence and quick thinking, most famously in the tale where it tricks crocodiles into forming a bridge by pretending to count them as it crosses. These stories transform the mousedeer’s physical vulnerability into a source of admiration, presenting it as a symbol of wit, adaptability, and resilience across communities that share its forests.

The mousedeer was also historically valued as a source of food, hunted across parts of Southeast Asia before wildlife protection measures were introduced from the mid-20th century onwards. Its meat was prized for its tenderness and was sometimes preserved as dendeng (spiced, dried meat). Today, although the Greater Mousedeer remains classified as Least Concern by the IUCN Red List, it faces continued pressures from habitat loss and hunting. The story of the mousedeer therefore reflects a long-standing relationship between humans and the forests they inhabit: a creature once hunted for sustenance and celebrated in folklore, now also recognised as part of the fragile ecosystems that sustain the region’s shared natural heritage.

objects.title: Kijang Gold Coins
objects.caption:
The old Kijang gold coins from Kelantan—including this kupang gold coin weighing around 0.64 g and inscribed with “Al Adil” in Arabic script—were once used as currency across the region. The deer (kijang) motif on these coins is traditionally associated with Che Siti Wan Kembang, the legendary queen said to have ruled the east coast of the Malay Peninsula in the 16th century, while also carrying broader cultural and symbolic meanings.

In Kelantanese Malay culture, the kijang represents qualities admired in rulers and leaders: grace, swiftness, vigilance, and strength. Its elegance and rarity made it a fitting emblem of royal identity, economic trust, and protection, while also distinguishing Kelantan’s coinage and state symbols from those of neighbouring regions. The kijang remains present today in the Kelantan State Emblem (Jata Negeri).

Kelantan and Pattani were historically connected through overlapping sultanates, dynastic ties, and trading networks, allowing symbols such as the kijang to circulate across political boundaries. The motif on these coins therefore reflects not only Kelantan’s royal heritage, but also the shared cultural connections that linked communities across the eastern Malay Peninsula.

objects.title: Nang Talung Puppetry Deer
objects.caption:
This shadow puppet in the form of a deer was crafted for Nang Talung, the shadow theatre tradition of Southern Thailand. Made from bovine or buffalo hide that has been scraped thin, sketched, and intricately carved, it is mounted on a single central bamboo control stick. During a performance, the Nai Nang (Puppet Master) manipulates the figure before a lit screen, casting its shadow onto a white cloth, while providing narration and vocalisation. The performance is accompanied by a musical ensemble featuring drums, thap (goblet drums), mong (gongs), ching (cymbals), and the Pi Chawa (Javanese oboe). The repertoire draws onIndian epics, namely the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, as well as indigenous local legends.

Nang Talung belongs to a family of shadow theatre traditions distributed across Southeast Asia under different names: Wayang Kulit in Malaysia, Wayang Purwa and other regional forms across Indonesia, Sbek Thom in Cambodia, and Nang Yai in the Chao Phraya River Basin. Across each of these traditions, animal-shaped puppets are essential for narrative completeness. Thus craftsmen draw fauna from both the natural environment familiar to each community and its literary repertoire. As this trail shows, the  deer has a deep presence in the region’s landscape and its stories. The kijang is embedded in Malay and Iban folklore as a figure of quickness, cunning, and spiritual power. The mousedeer Sang Kancil features in the Malay oral tradition as the most beloved trickster figure and the barking deer appears in Iban mythology as a powerful spirit. When the deer moves across the shadow screen, it brings something of its accumulated natural and symbolic life.

Beyond entertainment, shadow plays in Southeast Asia are integral to rituals of ancestral invocation, healing, and the exorcism of malevolent spirits. In Thailand, Nang Talung is traditionally performed between April and July, prior to the Buddhist Lent or the rainy season. The sacred context of the performance invests each animal figure — including the deer — with meaning that exceeds the narrative. Animal-shaped shadow puppets, in this sense, are more than props: they are the form through which shared beliefs about the natural and imagined world are given shape and set in motion.

objects.title: Bedil / Cannon with Dragon Motif
objects.caption:
During the 16th to 19th centuries, firearms were deeply integrated into the military, socio-economic, and ceremonial life of the Sultanate of Brunei. Their presence was documented as early as 1521 by Antonio Pigafetta, who noted bedil(portable firearms) and bronze cannons surrounding the Sultan’s palace. In these early centuries, cannons served primarily to defend national sovereignty, acting as vital strategic weapons during internal civil wars—such as the conflict between Sultan Abdul Hakkul Mubin and Pengiran Bendahara Muhyiddin—and against expanding foreign empires, including repelling two Spanish invasions during the reign of Sultan Bolkiah. Beyond the battlefield, these weapons occupied a central role in civilian life before the adoption of standardized currency. Cannons circulated as a primary medium of trade, where their value was calculated by both weight—measured in units of picul (equivalent to 133.3 pounds)—and the artistic quality of their carvings. They also functioned as instruments of customary law among the Dusun and Belait tribes to pay fines, served as required bridal gifts to secure marriage, and were fired from embankments as long-range communication tools to announce major events. Because cannon ownership signaled immense status, production was strictly controlled by the Sultan, who maintained a massive collection as a display of royal authority.

A magnificent example of this heritage is the dragon-shaped cannon, which seamlessly merges functional military technology with rich mythological symbolism. Bruneian cannons were crafted by pouring a molten alloy of copper and tin into clay molds, which cooled for two to three hours before being broken open for sculpting. While many cannons were simply carved with flora and fauna motifs, this particular piece goes further by embodying the creature itself: the gaping mouth forms the muzzle, a curled snout serves as the sight, the rear handle coils into a tail, and intricate metalwork details a spine ridge and scales throughout its body (now set on a modern mount). Across East and Southeast Asia, the dragon symbolized power, prosperity, and divine command over cosmic forces. In Borneo, the water-dragon was especially revered as a protective entity associated with rivers and the sea; for example, the Iban woven its image into textiles for spiritual protection. By casting artillery in this form, local artisans incorporated Chinese design elements into Malay decorative art, charging a weapon of foreign origin with the dragon's protective and destructive power and situating it within the local cosmological order—a choice of form that carried deep resonance when defending the Sultanate against foreign aggressors.

This artistic fusion was not isolated to Brunei, as carved guns and portable cannons bearing similar mythical motifs are found across Southeast Asia, including modern-day Indonesia, Thailand, and Myanmar. The widespread prevalence of these embellished weapons suggests that the dragon was a shared regional motif that communities across Southeast Asia drew upon as gunpowder technologies were systematically integrated into their military, social, and ceremonial systems.

objects.title: Blackened Brass Ritual Holy Water Vessel
objects.title_raw: Blackened Brass Ritual Holy Water Vessel
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This blackened brass holy water vessel from the Songkhla Lake basin reflects the meeting of metallurgy, Buddhist ritual practice, and the shared symbolic worlds of maritime Southeast Asia. Produced in a region shaped by centuries of trade and migration, the vessel combines Chinese decorative traditions with Theravada Buddhist ritual function, demonstrating how communities around the Southern Thai Peninsula adapted diverse artistic and spiritual traditions into local forms.

The vessel’s most prominent features are its twin dragon handles, cast on opposite sides of the body with their heads turned inward towards the rim. In Chinese traditions, the dragon (Long) was associated with imperial authority, prosperity, and control over water and rainfall. These meanings resonated strongly within Southeast Asia, where the Naga — the powerful serpent-like beings of Hindu-Buddhist traditions — similarly guarded rivers, lakes, and sources of fertility. In the water-dependent societies of the Songkhla Lake basin, the dragon and Naga shared a common symbolic role: as protectors of the waters that sustained human life.

The vessel’s other decorative elements reinforce this connection between spiritual protection and worldly wellbeing. Its base is formed by overlapping lotus petals, a Buddhist symbol of purity and enlightenment. Six low-relief panels around the body depict auspicious imagery including birds among blossoms, guardian lions, ducks among rice stalks, cranes beside bamboo, deer near plum blossoms, and egrets among aquatic plants. Together, these motifs express aspirations for longevity, prosperity, agricultural abundance, and harmony between humans and the natural world.

Within Theravada Buddhist practices, such holy water vessels would be used to hold Nam Phra Phutthamon (holy water), which is consecrated through monastic chanting and protective blessings. This sanctified water is sprinkled during auspicious ceremonies such as housewarmings, longevity rites, and the consecration of new buildings. The act of sprinkling holy water serves as a physical channel to convey divine blessings, spiritual safety, and peace to the participants. The dragons thus protected not only the vessel, but the sacred waters believed to connect human communities with spiritual forces.

The vessel’s hybrid style reflects the cosmopolitan character of the Songkhla Lake basin, where Chinese migrant communities, local Thai populations, and Buddhist institutions interacted through maritime trade networks. From the late Ayutthaya to early Rattanakosin periods, Chinese craftsmen and merchants contributed metalworking skills and decorative traditions that were incorporated into local religious objects. Wealthy merchants and community leaders often commissioned elaborate ritual vessels as temple offerings, transforming personal prosperity into acts of communal devotion.

objects.title: Canang
objects.caption:
This brass canang, a gong-like percussion instrument, was traditionally used in Brunei’s royal court as both a time marker and a means of announcing royal decrees or summons from the Sultan. It also played a role in ceremonial occasions, where its sound marked important moments within court life.

The canang is decorated with the image of the dragon, a motif that became prominent in Bruneian decorative arts through centuries of exchange with China. Across East and Southeast Asia, the dragon was associated with sovereignty, power, and protection, making it an appropriate symbol for an object connected with royal authority.

By placing the dragon on an instrument whose sound carried the presence of the ruler, this canang transformed a functional court object into a symbol of kingship itself. It reflects how artistic motifs travelled across maritime networks and were adopted into local royal traditions in Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Dragon-Shaped Mother-of-Pearl Inlaid Incense Tray
objects.caption:
This decorative incense tray features a dragon with its head held high, gazing upward with wide, bulging eyes, a short snout, and an open mouth. The body is straight, featuring a central rectangular compartment coated in red cinnabar lacquer (chat). The piece is supported by a rectangular base carved into dragon legs and claws, tapering off into a dragon's tail at the end.

It is hypothesized that this dragon-shaped tray was either a component of, or inspired by, the "Incense Clock" (Xiangpan), a traditional timekeeping device in Chinese culture. In such devices, incense was laid along a track — often referred to as a "Dragon Boat" — with metal weights suspended from threads at specific intervals. A metal tray was placed underneath. As the incense burned steadily to a thread, the weight would drop into the tray below, creating an audible chime to mark the time. These served as early "alarm clocks." Historical records from the 19th century (24th Buddhist Century) also indicate that Cantonese communities used these dragon incense trays as lighting stations for tobacco after evening meals.

The dragon form transformed this practical object into a statement of prestige. Across East and Southeast Asia, the dragon was associated with authority, prosperity, and command over cosmic forces, making it a powerful symbol of rulership and auspicious power. Its depiction on elite objects signalled refinement and status: here, the dragon’s raised head, powerful claws, and commanding posture elevate an everyday ritual object into one associated with cultivated taste and social distinction.

This prestige was further reinforced through its mother-of-pearl inlay, a highly skilled decorative technique historically associated with luxury craftsmanship. Developed in China over centuries and later adopted across mainland Southeast Asia, mother-of-pearl inlay travelled alongside artisans, trade networks, and communities, where it was adapted into local artistic traditions. The pairing of the dragon motif with this elite craft technique reflects the movement of both material knowledge and symbolic language across interconnected societies.

The significance of the dragon on this incense tray lies precisely in its ability to remain recognisable across borders. Whether appearing in Chinese courts or Southeast Asian elite households, the dragon continued to communicate power, prosperity, and auspicious protection. This object therefore represents the circulation of a shared visual language through which communities across and beyond Southeast Asia expressed status, aspiration, and connection to forces beyond the human world.
