objects.title: Flintlock Firearm
objects.caption:
This flintlock firearm distinguishes itself by its flared muzzle, shaped into the head of a dragon, with bulging eyes, fangs, and serrated edges lining the circumference of the mouth.

In the 17th and 18th centuries, the Dutch East India Company conducted diplomatic and trade relations with the Ayutthaya kingdom, exchanges that included the gifting of firearms. The Siamese court, which held a monopoly on the weapons trade and maintained gun control policies within Ayutthaya, received such objects into a very specific political context. The decision to adorn a firearm — likely of foreign make — with the head of a mythical serpent was, in that setting, is therefore an assertion of royal power and legitimacy. The specificity of the design suggests this was very likely a piece custom-made for local or regional tastes. Similar firearms were produced for the Chinese market, pointing to a broader practice of adapting the form of weapons to the symbolic vocabularies of their intended recipients.

At first glance, the pairing of a water-dwelling serpent with a weapon that produces fire and smoke may seem paradoxical. Yet, in Thai belief, its associations extend beyond water. Along the Mekong River, communities have long attributed the mysterious phenomenon of fireballs rising from the river’s surface to the Naga, calling them “Naga fireballs”.  Thus, the serpent is already, in the local imagination, a creature of fire as much as water. This incorporation of the serpent motif is all the more apt in light of the object's provenance. Received from the Royal Ceremonial Section of the Royal Palace, this firearm likely had ceremonial as well as military significance. Royal weapons in the Siamese court featured in rituals of allegiance, present at occasions where officials swore oaths to the king by drinking consecrated water prepared by monks. The naga's dominion over water would have made such weapons a natural presence in rituals where consecrated water was the medium of sacred oath.

That the dragon-headed firearm finds parallels across Southeast Asia and China speaks to the depth of the serpent's hold on the regional imagination – powerful enough, and revered enough, to be mobilised by communities across the region to communicate both martial and royal strength.

objects.title: Large Tile with Dragons
objects.caption:
According to Vietnamese origin traditions, the Vietnamese people are descended from the union of Lạc Long Quân, the Dragon Lord of Lạc, and Âu Cơ, the Mountain Fairy. Their children inherited both the qualities of the sea and the mountains, reflecting a worldview in which dragons connected different realms of nature. As beings associated with rivers, clouds, and subterranean waterways, dragons were believed to shape the landscape itself, with their presence sustaining the flow of life-giving energy (khí) through the earth.

This connection between dragons and the land is also reflected in the legend of Hạ Long Bay. When a young Vietnamese nation faced invasion from the sea, a mother dragon and her offspring descended to protect the people. They cast jewels that transformed into the islands and barriers that defended the coast. The story presents the dragon not only as a creature of power, but as a guardian whose presence protects both the people and the territory they inhabit.

This large earthenware tile from the Ly dynasty (1009–1225) embodies this powerful role of the dragon in Vietnamese imagination. The sinuous dragons, in vigorous movement amidst scrolling clouds, are typical of Ly dynasty art. Dragons have always had important symbolic and ritual meaning in Southeast Asia. During the Ly dynasty, the dragons adorned temples and palaces frequented by the king. Similar architectural elements in this style have been found at the ancient royal capital in Hanoi, formerly known as Thang Long (literally 'rising dragon').

The dragon’s prominence in Ly dynasty architecture reflects a wider Southeast Asian pattern in which mythical beings were closely tied to stories of origins, protection, and the ordering of the world. Across the region, dragon and serpent traditions often connected communities to the landscapes around them, expressing a belief that human societies were sustained through relationships with powerful forces of nature.

objects.title: Sunda Pangolin
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
The Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica) is a shy, nocturnal mammal native to the tropical forests of Southeast Asia. Enclosed in overlapping keratin scales, it resembles a living suit of armor and curls into an impenetrable ball when threatened. Preserved specimens at the Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum—mostly salvaged from accidental roadkill—offer visitors a rare, up-close look at this creature's unique anatomy. To combat local threats, the Singapore Pangolin Working Group was established in 2014, uniting government agencies, researchers, and community organizations to coordinate rescue efforts, habitat conservation, and public education.

Beyond modern ecology, the pangolin holds a fascinating place in traditional folklore due to its resemblance to mythical creatures—most notably the dragon. In classical East Asian texts, such as Li Shizhen’s Bencao Gangmu, the pangolin was referred to as lingli (“scaly carp”) and colloquially dubbed the “Earth Dragon” (Di Long). Because traditional dragons were portrayed as composite beasts covered in carp scales with power over subterranean realms, the pangolin—the world's only scale-covered mammal—was viewed as a living, terrestrial relative of the mythical beast. Its powerful claws and burrowing habits gave rise to legends that it navigated through a vast network of underground tunnels, cementing its image as a creature of protection, quiet resilience, and subterranean mastery.

Today, the Sunda pangolin is critically endangered. Driven by illegal wildlife trafficking for its meat and scales—falsely valued in traditional medicine—alongside rapid habitat fragmentation, wild populations face severe decline. High-profile transit seizures in Singapore highlight the global scale of wildlife crime, while climate change threatens the ant and termite populations vital to the pangolin's survival.

Bridging past and present, natural history and cultural heritage, the Sunda pangolin shows that animals in material culture are not just decorative motifs but storytellers carrying meaning across time. Through this remarkable creature, we can reflect on how cultural heritage can inspire conservation and care for endangered species. Protecting pangolins safeguards not only their lives but also the stories, creativity, and traditions they represent, preserving both natural and cultural heritage for future generations.

objects.title: Jar Decorated with Fish and a Beast
objects.title_raw: Jar Decorated with Fish and a Beast
objects.caption:
This large Vietnamese blue-and-white jar dated to the 14th century features two playful fish and a mythical aquatic beast. One fish devours another, while the mythical creature occupies the larger scene. Its aquatic form and elephant-like trunk make it recognisable as a makara commonly found in South and Southeast Asian myth and art. Its hybrid form places it between the worlds of animals, spirits, and the divine, as well as between land and water.

The painted decoration on this jar was likely inspired by Yuan-dynasty Chinese porcelain exported to the Southeast Asian region in the early 14th century. The fish and the lotus-petal borders are typical of Yuan wares, but seem to be rendered in an entirely free and distinct manner here. Jars like these were often used for storing valuable household goods such as wine, tea water, spices, medicines, and salted foods.

One of the largest known Vietnamese blue-and-white jars, it reflects the demand for finely crafted ceramics among Southeast Asia’s  elite communities. Similar jars discovered in Sulawesi reflect their movement through the maritime trade networks that connected Vietnam with island Southeast Asia. Along these routes, decorative forms and symbolic ideas travelled together: the fish, a familiar creature associated with water, fertility and abundance, appeared alongside the makara, a mythical guardian of aquatic realms shaped by Hindu-Buddhist and local regional traditions.

Produced in Vietnam, inspired by Chinese artistic vocabulary, and circulating to other parts of Southeast Asia, jars like this reflect the interconnected world of maritime Southeast Asia. Its surface brings together creatures from everyday experience and mythical imagination. The jar shows how communities across the region shared and transformed images of the waters that connected them.

objects.title: Rostrum of the Largetooth Sawfish
objects.caption:
The Largetooth Sawfish (Pristis pristis) is a large marine elasmobranch — a relative of rays — distinguished by its elongated, flattened snout known as a rostrum. This rostrum is lined with bilateral transverse teeth, resembling a double-sided saw. Historically, sawfish were prevalent across tropical Indo-Pacific waters, including Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Uniquely euryhaline, they possess the physiological capacity to transition between marine, brackish, and freshwater environments, often inhabiting major river systems and estuaries.

In Southeast Asian folk belief, the rarity and formidable appearance of the sawfish elevated it to the status of a guardian spirit. In the Kinabatangan River basin of Sabah, Malaysia, the rostrum is nailed above doorways as an apotropaic talisman. When wrapped in cloth and hung over a cradle, it is believed to pacify restless infants. In Dondai village at Lake Sentani in Papua, Indonesia, the sawfish is a totemic animal whose flesh is taboo to consume. Traditional architecture there features house posts carved with sawfish motifs to commemorate maritime ancestors. The sawfish also appears in indigenous bark paintings as a visual record of natural and spiritual heritage.

Sawfish populations in Southeast Asian waters are now classified as Critically Endangered (CR) on the IUCN Red List (2022). The sawfish’s unique physical appearance makes them highly vulnerable to entanglement in fishing nets. Today, despite their declining presence in nature, sawfish are harvested for their meat, their skin is processed into leather, and their rostra are used in traditional medicine. Furthermore, their cultural significance as wood saws, talismans, and home decorations endures as part of the region’s shared beliefs and practice.

objects.title: Skeleton of Singapore’s First Recorded Sperm Whale (Physeter macrocephalus)
objects.title_raw: Skeleton of Singapore’s First Recorded Sperm Whale  (Physeter macrocephalus)
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
Discovered drifting off the coast of Jurong Island in July 2015, this 10.6-metre adult female — named Jubi Lee, in honour of the year Singapore celebrated its golden jubilee — offers rare insight into the marine ecosystems of Southeast Asia. Her remains tell a powerful story: ship-strike injuries, squid beaks, and tragically, pieces of plastic, which serve as reminders of both the richness of our oceans, as well as the profound impact human activity leaves behind.

Divers from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore first secured the specimen before towing it carefully across the West Johor Strait to the Tuas Marine Transfer Station. Here museum scientists began the process of examination, dissection, and recovery. She was introduced to the public on 15 March 2016. The large diversity of deep-sea prey items found in her gut suggests she had been hunting in waters well beyond Singapore and its surrounding enclosed seas before her death. An analysis of her stomach contents reveal that she may have originated from a population in the Indian Ocean, near the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Indonesia.

Southeast Asia’s waters continue to support several species of whales. Humpback whales, classified as Least Concern by the IUCN, have been recorded off the coasts of the Philippines and Thailand between October and January, when they migrate to warmer waters for breeding. Sperm whales, classified as Vulnerable, have been observed around Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, and Cambodia, where they feed and reproduce. Bryde’s whales — often called “tropical whales” due to their preference for warmer waters above 15°C — have also been recorded in Thailand, Indonesia, and Brunei. Together, these species reflect the importance of Southeast Asia’s seas as part of wider migratory and ecological networks.

That this sperm whale skeleton should find a place of prominence in a museum is, in the context of Southeast Asia, less a modern invention than a continuation of something older. On the island of Lembata in eastern Indonesia, whale skulls were once venerated in temples much like the bones of ancestors. The hunt itself was considered a sacred act. Along the coast of Vietnam, hunting whales was taboo since they were regarded as protectors. A major temple dated to 1762 was even dedicated to the whale deity known as 'Lord Fish'. Emperors of the Nguyen dynasty conferred titles upon whales in the 19th century. Jubi Lee's place in the museum, shaped by science rather than ritual, is a different kind of honour. Having said this, the impulse to mark the whale as significant, and to preserve its significance for a community, is one the region has long known and shared.

Through research, preservation, and education, the LKCNHM continues to turn these discoveries into lessons for future generations.

objects.title: Spotted White Eagle Ray Bone (Aetobatus ocellatus)
objects.title_raw: Spotted White Eagle Ray Bone (Aetobatus ocellatus)
objects.caption:
The spotted white eagle ray (Aetobatus ocellatus) is a marine animal recognised by its smooth skin, white spots scattered across its back, and white underside. Its body is shaped like a rhombus, allowing it to swim freely as if it were a bird in flight. It features one to six barbs located near the base of its long, slender tail. Some species have venomous spines at the tail's base.

The eagle ray can reach a width of 1.5 metres, with a maximum recorded width of 3 metres and a weight of 230 kilograms. Its habitat spans the Pacific, Indian, and Atlantic Oceans, though it may also enter brackish water near river mouths to feed The spotted white eagle ray uses its mouth to dig into the sandy seabed in search of shells, shrimp, mantis shrimp, and crabs.

The stingray tail, equipped with natural barbs, followed its own unique cultural path across Southeast Asia. It was once used as a whip for punishment, and was later adapted into short, knife-like defensive tools in Southern Thailand and other parts of the region. Eagle rays were also traditionally prepared as shredded grilled stingray for Khao Chae, a dish created by the Thai-Mon community and offered to monks during Songkran as a gesture of auspiciousness and renewal. Stingray skin, valued for its naturally rough texture, was processed as a material for sword hilts, providing superior grip and exceptional durability. The ray also served as an ingredient in Chinese medicine.

Today, the spotted eagle ray faces increasing threats from these long-standing uses as well as modern environmental pressures. Targeted fishing, combined with bycatch from fishing methods that indiscriminately capture marine species, has contributed to declining populations. The degradation of coral reefs and shifting marine ecosystems have further reduced its food sources and habitats. As a result of these combined pressures, the species was classified as Endangered on the 2023 IUCN Red List.

objects.title: Stingray Barb Dagger
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This dagger's blade is a stingray's caudal spine, known in Thai as the ngiang or the serrated defensive barb. It is mounted on a handle fashioned from animal horn and hand-polished to ensure a secure, ergonomic grip. Naturally rigid, exceptionally sharp, and flanked by retroverted, saw-like serrations, the spine functions as a devastating weapon. Its overall architecture allows it to pierce soft tissue effortlessly upon thrusting, while its backward-facing barbs cause extensive, jagged lacerations upon extraction. Deliberately minimalist yet structurally robust, it reflects how Southern Thai folk artisans prioritised utility and durability. Coastal fishermen, seafarers, and maritime nomads (Chao Lay) carried such compact daggers as weapons for self-defence during long-distance maritime voyages.

Beyond its physical lethality, the stingray barb dagger is deeply rooted in the worldview of seafaring and fishing communities. Due to the highly painful venom delivered by live stingray barbs, folk belief attributes an inherent spiritual potency to the bone itself. Consequently, it was carried as an active talisman, believed to be capable of neutralising hazards and warding off malevolent spirits. According to regional esoteric lore, because the spine has never been melted, smelted, or altered by human fire, it retains a state of "primordial purity", which elevates it from a tactical weapon into a spiritual amulet.

Indigenous documentation, including traditional folding books (Samut Khoi) and classical treatises on military strategy (Tamra Pichai Songkhram), categorises weapons crafted from raw organic matter such as bone, antler, and horn as "non-ferrous weaponry" (awut nok rabop lek). The latter is a recognised martial tradition outside the iron metallurgy system.

This dagger’s discovery in Pattani, a historical maritime emporium on the eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula, places it within a trade-port culture. Here coastal communities were required to arm and protect themselves in complex, multi-ethnic commercial environments. The fact that communities across the Malay Peninsula drew on the same animal for the same purpose reflects a shared martial and spiritual vocabulary, rooted in the creatures of the water they held in common.

objects.title: Sukhothai Celadon Bowl Fragment with Fish Design (Ceramic Shard)
objects.title_raw: Sukhothai Celadon Bowl Fragment with Fish Design  (Ceramic Shard)
objects.caption:
This fragment of a glazed earthenware bowl, dated to around the 16th century, is decorated with black underglaze painting beneath a transparent glaze. At the interior base, four spur marks appear at the centre: these traces are left by supports used during the kiln-firing process to prevent the vessels from sticking together. Within two concentric circles, a single fish motif faces right, accompanied by an inscription in Sukhothai Thai script reading “Mae Pla Ka”. The rim carries simple black painted lines. The fragment was donated to the National Museum Bangkok in 1976.

The fish depicted on the bowl is a Siamese fighting fish (Pangasius gigas), a freshwater fish similar to the common carp. It has a stout, bulging body, a tall dorsal fin, and two pairs of barbels around its mouth. Its body is black or dark brown with small, reddish scales. The caudal fin is deeply forked. This fish typically feeds on the bottom, grazing on algae and seaweed. It can be found in rivers and freshwater sources throughout Thailand. In general, the fish motif suggested fertility and abundance. It became popular amongst the Sukhothai potters of the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.

This glazed vessel exhibits the technique of applying black patterns under the clear glaze, a style prevalent in the mid-Sukhothai pottery production period to which it belongs. The black pattern was created using iron rust. This technique has been found at the Koh Noi kiln sites in Si Satchanalai and the Sukhothai city site, alongside vessels using other techniques such as brown-black and bluish-green glazes.

With the fish, the marks left by the kiln-firing process also became part of the vessel’s final appearance. The spur supports used to separate vessels during firing left impressions on the base. Whereas the mottled surface of the fish, partially hiding the appearance of the spurs, blended the potter’s decoration and the technical processes of production. The image therefore carries traces not only of artistic intention, but also of the craft methods that brought it into being.

Although the journey of this particular fragment remains unknown, vessels like this were widely circulated through Southeast Asia’s maritime trade networks. During the Ming dynasty, restrictions on private Chinese ceramic exports in the 14th to 16th centuries reduced the availability of Chinese wares in some markets. This led to increased demand for ceramics from production centres in Burma, Thailand, and Vietnam. Thai ceramics, particularly high-quality glazed wares from Sukhothai, moved across the region. Many examples have been recovered from shipwrecks including the Longquan wreck (c. 1400), as well as the Ko Khram and Rayong wrecks (1380-1500). These ships and trade networks reveal how local ceramic technologies and riverine fish imagery became part of a shared material culture that travelled across and perhaps even beyond Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Vessel in the Form of a Fish
objects.title_raw: Vessel in the Form of a Fish
objects.caption:
This two-tone glazed stoneware vessel, dated to around the 12th century, takes the form of a fish, with its body glazed green and its fins and tail finished in brown. The vessel is carefully modelled with defined eyes, scales, and a mouth formed as a circular opening for pouring. It may have been used as a sprinkler vessel, possibly for pouring lustral water in ritual settings.

Across Southeast Asia, fish have long been associated with fertility, abundance, and the life-giving qualities of water. According to the Royal Chronicles of Ayutthaya, when King U-Thong, the first monarch of Ayutthaya, was seeking a site for his capital, he encountered plentiful fish in the waters around Nong Sano and chose the location as an auspicious sign.

By shaping a practical pouring vessel in the form of a fish, these associations are brought into everyday use. Each act of pouring transformed the vessel from a simple container into a reminder of the region’s shared connections with water and its abundant creatures.

objects.title: Wooden Chalk-Line Reels (Marking Gauges)
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
The Rang That (also known as Phrok That) is an antique traditional woodworking marking tool used by master carpenters to snap straight, highly accurate reference lines onto raw timber before sawing, hewing, or joinery. It constituted a foundational implement for ancient builders across the Southern Thai peninsula. It was used in the construction of vernacular stilt houses, traditional seafaring, domestic furniture, and everyday woodenware.

While a standard Rang That exhibits a minimalist rectangular geometry, craftsmen across the region frequently sculpted these wooden tools into zoomorphic forms. The two specimens displayed here — one shaped like a snake and the other like fish — balance playful artistry with everyday industrial utility.

Internally, the tool is divided into two chambers: a reeling chamber housing a spool of fine cotton thread attached to a manual turning crank (Mue Muan), and a pigment well packed with raw cotton saturated in carbon lampblack (Khamau Dam) mixed with water. To use it, the carpenter draws the thread out across the timber, passing it through the lampblack-soaked well. Once the black-coated thread is pulled taut against the wood, the craftsman pinches the midpoint, pulls it vertically upward, and snaps it back down. He thus transfers a razor-sharp, uniform straight line onto the surface. The crank can then be rotated to retract the cord back into the wooden body.

Despite its simple construction, the Rang That reflects a sophisticated understanding of materials and mechanics. By using hardwood, cotton thread, and carbon soot produced from everyday domestic resources, craftsmen created a reliable precision instrument adapted to local building practices. The Southern dialect preserves the shared presence of this tool in its idioms: "Dam Muean Rang That" ("as black as a carpenter's chalk-line reel") became a common metaphor for an exceptionally deep, sun-darkened complexion, a phrase that could only have currency in a society where this tool was present in every workshop.

This fish-shaped Rang That is thus a demonstration of how technological knowledge and environmental familiarity were intertwined in traditional Southeast Asian craftsmanship. By adapting a precision tool to the form of a creature from their coastal surroundings, craftsmen connected the practical demands of construction with the landscapes and livelihoods that sustained them.

objects.title: Badau
objects.caption:
The badau is a traditional weapon of the Murut people of Brunei Darussalam. Given the Murut's historical reputation as skilled warriors, it is likely that the craftsmanship and use of the badau developed alongside their martial traditions. However, further historical and ethnographic research is needed to substantiate this relationship. Similar in form to a machete, it was historically used both as a tool and a weapon. Its handle is carved with the head of the Rhinoceros Hornbill (Buceros rhinoceros), complete with the species’ distinctive, large beak.

Among the Murut, hornbills are regarded as sacred birds. Strict taboos surrounded the hunting of the Helmeted Hornbill and Rhinoceros Hornbill. It was believed that harming these birds could bring misfortune, including blindness or cholera. By carving the hornbill’s form rather than using materials from the bird itself, the badau therefore embodies a relationship of respect and protection: the animal’s spiritual power is invoked through representation, while the creature remains unharmed.

This reverence for the hornbill extends across Borneo’s communities. Among the Dayak peoples of Kalimantan and the Iban of Sarawak, the hornbill similarly occupies an important place in ceremonial objects and spiritual traditions. As a native species of the island, its presence transcends ethnic and political boundaries, linking communities through shared understandings of the bird’s power and protection.

objects.title: Calapa with Bird Motif
objects.caption:
This container for storing betel leaves, areca nuts (locally known as pinang), tobacco (sigup), and jewellery was used when guests came to visit and during gatherings such as weddings and thanksgiving ceremonies, as well as in everyday use. Shaped with a bird design featuring large wings and a spread tail, the calapa is an object whose form invites interpretation.

The design may be inspired by the Rhinoceros Hornbill, a species native to Borneo and a common presence in Brunei Darussalam. The long, curved beak and the prominent structure rising above the head closely resemble the hornbill's distinctive casque, suggesting the craftsman may have drawn on the most familiar and culturally significant bird of the local landscape. At the same time, the calapa may reflect the influence of the peacock, a bird whose elaborate plumage and regal bearing have inspired art across much of Southeast Asia. Peacocks are not native to Brunei Darussalam, however, and their appearance here likely speaks to the influence of artistic traditions carried along the trade networks that long connected Brunei to the wider Malay and Indian Ocean worlds.

Whether peacock, hornbill, or an imaginative synthesis of both, the bird form chosen for a vessel of hospitality speaks to the way Southeast Asian decorative traditions have long drawn on the natural world, and on the movement of forms and ideas across borders, to give meaning to everyday objects. In the context of Brunei's traditional life, a container associated with generosity and ceremony is a fitting vehicle for the image of the hornbill. For, the bird’s associations with protection and vitality run deep across the communities of Borneo.

objects.title: Copper Pot
objects.caption:
This traditional copper pot is decorated with fine circular engravings encircling the body and lid, a raised line at the centre of the body, and motifs of birds alongside Islamic calligraphy. Such pots are used in daily life for cooking rice and preparing traditional medicine, including decoctions of leaves and roots.

The bird motifs on this vessel, including the hornbill, carry associations of protection and vitality deeply rooted in the beliefs of Borneo’s communities. Across Brunei and the wider Borneo island, the hornbill has long been understood as a guardian figure, messenger of the upper world, and symbol of life force -- as such, in this case the pot that prepares the medicine can then transfer its protective charge to the remedy itself.

The Islamic calligraphy engraved alongside the bird motifs reflects the layered spiritual world of Brunei's material culture, where indigenous animist beliefs and Islamic faith have coexisted and inflected one another across centuries. In this vessel, the protective associations of the hornbill and the blessing invoked through sacred script reinforce one another in a single object designed for everyday cooking and healing.

This copper pot reflects a wider Southeast Asian pattern in which everyday objects bring together practical knowledge, spiritual beliefs, and relationships with the natural world. Through the hornbill motif, which finds its origin in animistic beliefs, as well as Islamic inscriptions, a domestic vessel becomes a bearer of protection and healing.

objects.title: Iban’s Hornbill Image
objects.caption:
Depictions of the rhinoceros hornbill, called kenyalang, are among the most spectacular carvings produced by the Iban people. Made from wood and pigments, this figure holds a fig in its beak — a detail whose shape deliberately resembles a trophy head, calling to mind the headhunting traditions of Iban society. Hornbills like this were carved for the sacred ceremony of Gawai Kenyalang, originally associated with fighting, raiding, and headhunting, but which today endures as a thanksgiving celebration.

For the Iban, the hornbill is considered the chief of birds and a messenger of the deities in the upper world, representing the vital life force present in all living beings. Communities believed they could invoke the hornbill’s assistance in warfare, calling upon its power to carry their intentions into the divine realm. More broadly, among the Dayak peoples of Borneo, the hornbill holds a place of highest reverence as a sacred intermediary and a bearer of good omens. Dayak tradition further holds that the intricate designs on hornbill carvings are not created solely through human skill, but are guided by divine inspiration.

Central to the cosmology of this carving is the figure of Sengalang Burong, the Brahminy Kite who in Iban belief is venerated as their ancestor, and whose messages are carried by the hornbill. During Gawai Kenyalang, held after the harvest in Sengalang’s honour, a carving such as this would be mounted on a tall pole, surrounded by offerings of food and sacred incantations. Positioned at the centre of the ceremony, the kenyalang gave physical form to the community’s relationship with the upper world and the spiritual forces believed to sustain it.

The kenyalang reflects an Iban worldview in which animals are active participants in relationships between humans, ancestors, and the divine. Although expressed through a distinctly Iban tradition, the reverence of the hornbill echoes wider, shared Southeast Asian understandings of animals as sources of spiritual power, protection, and connection.

objects.title: Kalimantan War Helmet
objects.caption:
This war commander's helmet, or katapu, represents the Dayak people's ingenuity in merging earthly and celestial powers for protection on the battlefield. Its base is crafted from tightly woven Bornean rattan, strong enough to deflect enemy arrows and mandau sword slashes. Set above this practical shell of armour is a rhinoceros hornbill (burung enggang) skull, placed to symbolise protection provided by spirits of the sky.

In Dayak belief, the hornbill embodies the Panglima Burung (Bird Commander), a mystical figure who emerges during warfare to instil battlefield confidence. By fixing the hornbill's skull to the crown of the helmet, the wearer brought this protective spirit into direct physical contact with his own person. Thus he situated himself simultaneously within the practical and the cosmic dimensions of battle.

The inclusion of premium embellishments such as hornbill skulls, feathers, intricate beadwork, and mirrors indicates that this specific katapu was reserved exclusively for elite figures such as tribal chiefs or war commanders. During this era, beads and mirrors were rare luxury items that served as distinct markers of high social status. In parallel, the spiritual protection and association with upper-world spirits afforded by the hornbill was commensurate with that authority.

The hornbill, whose home is the forest canopy—a threshold between the human world and the sky — was an ideal symbol for this connection. Through the katapu, the bird’s presence linked the warrior not only to the protection of ancestral and spiritual forces, but also to the living landscape and the region that sustained Dayak communities.

objects.title: Oriental Pied Hornbill and Rhinoceros Hornbill
objects.title_raw: Oriental Pied Hornbill and Rhinoceros Hornbill
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, Singapore
objects.caption:
These two species — the Oriental Pied Hornbill (Anthracoceros albirostris) and the Rhinoceros Hornbill (Buceros rhinoceros) — belong to a family of birds instantly recognisable by their large, curved bills and prominent casques, the hollow structures rising above their beaks. Of the 59 extant hornbill species worldwide, 31 are found in Asia, where they inhabit tropical forests. Their powerful bills allow them to consume large fruits and a wide range of other foods, while their role as seed dispersers helps sustain the regeneration and diversity of forest ecosystems.

Beyond their ecological importance, hornbills have generated some of the richest symbolic and ceremonial traditions among the communities of Borneo. While both specimens represent the hornbill family, it is the Rhinoceros Hornbill that holds the most prominent cultural role across the island. Known as the kenyalang among the Iban of Sarawak and as burung enggang among the Dayak peoples of Kalimantan, it is regarded as the chief of birds and a messenger of the deities in the upper world. The bird is believed to embody the vital life force present in all living beings, serving as an intermediary between the human and spiritual realms by carrying prayers, and granting protection to those who honour it.

In Dayak traditions, the hornbill is also associated with the Panglima Burung (“Bird Commander”), a mystical guardian figure invoked during warfare to inspire courage and protection. Its skull and feathers were incorporated into the ceremonial attire and weapons of chiefs and warriors, while its image appears on everyday and ritual objects such as copper pots, storage vessels, and ceremonial containers
Today, hornbills face increasing threats across Southeast Asia. The Oriental Pied Hornbill is classified as Least Concern by the IUCN, partly due to its ability to survive in a wider range of habitats, while the Rhinoceros Hornbill is classified as Vulnerable. Across the region, populations are threatened by habitat loss and degradation caused by deforestation, agricultural expansion, unsustainable logging, mining, and fires, as well as illegal hunting and trade. The decline of hornbills therefore represents not only a loss of biodiversity, but also the erosion of cultural relationships that have connected communities with these remarkable birds for generations.

Yet, conservation efforts also demonstrate that these relationships can be renewed. In Singapore, where the Oriental Pied Hornbill was once considered extinct, populations were successfully re-established through efforts such as the installation of artificial nest boxes.

objects.title: Cast Brass Tabletop Horse - Shaped Lighter
objects.title_raw: Cast Brass Tabletop Horse - Shaped Lighter
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This cast brass horse-shaped tabletop lighter integrates modern ignition technology with decorative metal sculpture. Freestanding, the horse is cast entirely from solid brass (Thong Luang). Careful attention is paid to the fine details of the mane, flowing tail, structured saddle, and decorative bridle, thus demonstrating a skilled blending of artistic form and everyday function. Built directly into the horse's back is a mechanical ignition assembly consisting of a thumb lever, a flint housing, and a burner cap, a spring-loaded mechanism that became globally popular during the mid-twentieth century.

Brass was well suited to this object, allowing artisans to capture fine sculptural detail while retaining the durability required of a functional device. By concealing an industrial mechanism within the body of an auspicious animal, the lighter transformed modern technology into an object of display. This reflects a wider trend in Southern Thai society: a period of rapid modernisation and expanding global trade, when household objects increasingly served not only practical purposes but also expressed wealth, taste, and cosmopolitan identity.

Originally used to ignite cigarettes, cigars, or candles, this lighter would have occupied a prominent place in reception rooms, offices, and household spaces, where it functioned as both a convenience and a statement of modern lifestyle. This was especially significant in Hat Yai, Songkhla Province, where post-war growth driven by railway connections, rubber production, and trade transformed the city into a major commercial centre linking Southern Thailand with Penang, Singapore, and wider maritime markets. As mechanical lighters replaced earlier methods using hearth embers, oil lamps, or flint-and-steel tools, they became part of new forms of hospitality, social exchange, and business interaction.

Yet the horse form shows that modern technology was not adopted in isolation from older systems of meaning. Across Chinese and Southeast Asian traditions, the horse symbolised vitality, endurance, speed, and success. By combining a modern ignition mechanism with an auspicious animal form, this object turned an industrial device into a symbol of progress and aspiration.

Donated by a merchant family from Hat Yai, this lighter preserves a moment when imported technologies entered Southern Thai households and were given new local meanings. The horse-shaped form reveals how communities across maritime Southeast Asia reshaped modern technologies through familiar symbols. They turned globally shared technologies into expressions of local identity and ambition.

objects.title: Dastar / Head Cloth with Horse Motif
objects.title_raw: Dastar / Head Cloth with Horse Motif
objects.caption:
This dastar cloth is woven using the tanggam bajang (dovetail) technique and made from cotton threads. It features a horse-rider motif alongside geometric patterns. The cloth is traditionally worn as a head adornment by Bajau and Kadazandusun men during customary ceremonies and festive celebrations in Sabah. This piece originates from Kota Belud, Sabah, and dates to around the 1940s.

The horse-rider motif in Bajau and Kadazandusun textiles is rich in meaning. It likely symbolizes social prestige and masculinity, as well as the strength and identity of horse-riding communities. The motif also conveys vitality, movement, leadership, nobility, and communal pride. The Bajau of Kota Belud are well known for their horse-riding culture and are sometimes referred to as the "cowboys of the East." Horses represent markers of social status and physical strength, and this connection is most visible in ceremony. In contexts such as marriage celebrations, riding a horse is a display of skill, bravery, and prestige; according to cultural records, during Bajau wedding processions the groom may ride a horse to the bride's home as a symbol of his strength and status.

In weaving and textile arts, such motifs preserve this heritage in fabric. Worn on the head, which is the most visible and honoured part of the body, the dastar carries the horse-rider motif into the ceremonial space during formal occasions. A community's relationship with the horse, lived on horseback and expressed in ceremony, is here encoded in thread.

objects.title: Liturgical Pulpit Covers (Koh Yo Brocade Textile)
objects.title_raw: Liturgical Pulpit Covers (Koh Yo Brocade Textile)
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.material: Supplemented supplementary-weft (Yok Dok) handwoven cotton, embellished with antique Southern glass beads
objects.local_name: Pha Hum Thammasan / ผ้าหุ้มธรรมมาสน (ผ้าทอเกาะยอ)
objects.object_biography: Original Heirloom Piece: Transferred via ritual donation by Phra Athikan Prathom Pathamo, the late Abbot of Wat Thai Yo, from Village No. 8, Koh Yo Sub-district, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province. Accessioned into the permanent collection vaults of the Folklore Museum on 9 October 2014. Modern Replica Piece: Hand-loomed and donated by Ms. Ubolsri Attaphan, sourced from Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla Province. Exhibited in the Local Textile Exhibition Room (Hong Pha Tho Pheurm Mueang), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This liturgical pulpit cover from the historic Thai temple of Wat Thai Yo, Songkhla Province, was woven using the intricate Yok Dok (supplementary weft) technique. It created raised patterns in saffron yellow, emerald green, and charcoal black against a deep red ground. Originally made in 1934 as an offering to the temple, such textiles were considered acts of merit-making (Bun), with laywomen dedicating their labour, skill, and devotion to supporting the Buddhist community. Hung around the preaching pulpit (Thammasan), the cloth transformed the space of the sermon into a sacred setting for the transmission of the Dhamma.

Among its woven designs are two powerful animal forms: the Royal Garuda (Krut) and sacred steeds (Ma). Both are depicted as celestial vehicles associated with movement between earthly and higher realms. The Garuda, the divine mount of Vishnu in Hindu-Buddhist traditions, carries associations of power, protection, and heavenly authority. The horse, long associated across Southeast Asia with nobility, strength, and martial ability, similarly represents a vehicle of elevation and prestige. Together, these animals frame Buddhist devotion through images of ascent, guardianship, and spiritual aspiration.

In addition, the colours of the textile also highlight the community's use of localised natural resources. The dyes were drawn entirely from local organic sources: red from the iron-rich earthen clays of Koh Yo's hillsides, yellow extracted from jackfruit heartwood, and black from fermented ebony berries. These colours were traditionally reserved for ritual objects across the region, symbolising spiritual protection, dynastic prosperity, and cosmic blessing.

The textile also preserves the identity of the community that created it. Using the Yok Dok technique, weavers incorporated the names of the women who sponsored and produced the cloth directly into its structure, thus turning the textile into a record of collective devotion. The creation of such elaborate temple offerings was a means through which lay communities accumulated merit, transforming everyday skills such as weaving into acts of religious service.

The Pha Hum Thammasan demonstrates how animal imagery travelled across South and Southeast Asian religious traditions while acquiring local meanings through community action. In this textile, the Garuda and horse serve as sacred vehicles woven into an offering through which the community expressed faith, identity, and its relationship with the Buddhist cosmos.

objects.title: Nang Talung Puppetry Horse
objects.caption:
This shadow puppet in the form of a horse was crafted for Nang Talung, the shadow theatre tradition of Southern Thailand. Made from bovine or buffalo hide that has been scraped thin, sketched, and intricately carved, it is mounted on a single central bamboo control stick. During a performance, the Nai Nang (Puppet Master) manipulates the figure before a lit screen, casting its shadow onto a white cloth, while providing narration and vocalisation. The performance is accompanied by a musical ensemble featuring drums, thap (goblet drums), mong (gongs), ching (cymbals), and the Pi Chawa (Javanese oboe). The repertoire draws onIndian epics, namely the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, as well as indigenous local legends.

Nang Talung belongs to a family of shadow theatre traditions distributed across Southeast Asia under different names: Wayang Kulit in Malaysia, Wayang Purwa and other regional forms across Indonesia, Sbek Thom in Cambodia, and Nang Yai in the Chao Phraya River Basin. Across each of these traditions, animal-shaped puppets are essential for narrative completeness. Thus craftsmen draw fauna from both the natural environment familiar to each community and its literary repertoire. The horse is one of many such animals drawn more from the literary than the natural repertoire.

As such horses were not native to Southeast Asia but arrived early on from as far as the Middle East, India, China and Mongolia via overland and maritime routes. Horses were known in Thailand since at least the Dvaravati period (6th–11th centuries CE), evidenced by archaeological finds and their frequent depiction in works of art — including an ivory comb from Chansen, Nakhon Sawan Province, carved with images of two horses and auspicious motifs. Horse imagery was employed in the decoration of utilitarian objects, personal ornaments, architectural stucco reliefs, and narrative scenes associated with Buddhism, a tradition that continued into the Lopburi period (11th–13th centuries CE). Closely associated with rulers and kingship, and important in religious literature and visual culture, the horse likely accompanied royal characters in shadow-play performances. When this puppet would have moved across the screen, it carried with it a long association between horses, sovereignty, and the sacred.

objects.title: Oracle Bone
objects.caption: These buffalo bones are inscribed on both sides. The concave face is inscribed with symbols of fish, seven-point stars, stylized lizards, and human motifs, while the convex face features Batak script. These bones were most likely amulets made by magician-priests to be worn by the Batak people for protection, granting additional powers during hunting and battles, and warding off evil spirits and illnesses. Such amulets were often made of animal bones—usually a buffalo rib or long bone cut into small cylindrical forms. The inscriptions are highlighted with a black, ink-like substance to reveal the magic formulae, motifs, and astrological signs. Batak heritage is thought to be rooted in ancient Austronesian culture, influenced by Indian communities who settled in the Barus area as early as the 7th century, as well as Hindu-Buddhist traditions emanating from ritual centers such as Padang Lawas in North Sumatra.

objects.title: Traditional Maritime Boxes (Chased Hardwood Storage Caskets) in Horse Design
objects.title_raw: Traditional Maritime Boxes (Chased Hardwood Storage Caskets)  in Horse Design
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
Compact wooden storage chest used by communities along the Southern Thai coast for safeguarding vital provisions during deep-sea voyages. Local woodworkers selected high-density, resinous indigenous hardwoods such as Kiam wood (Cotylelobium lanceolatum) and Lumpho wood (Intsia palembanica) for their natural resistance to rot, humidity, and marine brine. The box's low-set, elongated rectangular silhouette was engineered for absolute equilibrium on the deck of a rolling vessel, preventing sliding or inversion during heavy monsoonal swells. Its lid was turned on a primitive wood lathe to ensure a hermetic friction fit, and many specimens featured tongue-and-groove slide locks or rattan tie-down cords to block sea spray. This impeccable design kept the contents of the box—tobacco, nipa palm wrapper leaves, fire-striking apparatus, currency, and family documents— bone-dry across multi-day expeditions.

What elevates the Ko-Ta into a work of folk art is its zoomorphic carving. In the equine-form box, the horse symbolises muscular power, speed, endurance, and safe passage. Fishermen who spent their lives on water rather than land chose the horse as a spiritual companion, one that allowed the vessel to gallop across cresting ocean waves with the courage needed to survive long voyages.

Strict taboos governed the Ko-Ta onboard: under no circumstances could it be stored upside down; it had to be placed completely upright with its lid facing the heavens, a sympathetic charm ensuring stable sailing and smooth fortune. The name's Malay-Thai linguistic root, and the object's presence across Southern Thai coastal communities whose lives were shaped by the same maritime networks as the wider Malay world, reflects a shared material culture. Here practical engineering, animal symbolism, and the logic of survival at sea were inseparable.

objects.title: A Sandstone Lintel depicting Vishnu Anantashayana (Vishnu reclining on the serpent Ananta)
objects.title_raw: A Sandstone Lintel depicting Vishnu Anantashayana  (Vishnu reclining on the serpent Ananta)
objects.caption:
According to Hindu belief, particularly in the Puranas, before creation begins, the Hindu god Vishnu reclines in meditation upon the endless serpent Ananta in the cosmic Ocean of Milk (Kshira Sagara), from which the universe is renewed. This ocean is also the setting of the great churning myth, when gods and demons used the serpent Vasuki as a rope to churn the waters in search of amrita, the nectar of immortality. Through these stories, serpents and aquatic beings became associated with the forces that sustain creation: water, fertility, cosmic balance, and renewal.

This sandstone lintel from 12th-century Lopburi art depicts "Vishnu Anantasayin," which means "the reclining of Vishnu upon the serpent Ananta”. Unusually, the carving gives prominence to the makara, a mythical aquatic creature with features drawn from multiple animals, which represents the cosmic waters surrounding Vishnu. Such imagery reflects the movement of Hindu-Buddhist ideas across South and Southeast Asia, where creatures of water and serpent forms were repeatedly adapted into local artistic traditions.

The serpent and makara reveal a shared regional imagination in which animals from rivers, oceans, and mythical realms became symbols of the forces that shaped life itself, connecting landscapes, cosmology, and communities across Asia.

objects.title: Balinese Naga Corbels
objects.caption:
In Balinese culture, the mythical serpent known as the Nāga is a vital guardian woven into the island’s architectural, spiritual, and artistic identity. This symbolism spans from art institutions to sacred water sites. At the Ada Guna Museum in Bali, for instance, elaborate Naga-shaped corbels feature alongside figures of Garuda and Singha (lion), serving as striking decorative and structural elements that reflect the museum’s dedication to preserving family architectural collections and traditional craftsmanship.

Architecturally, Nāgas fulfill both functional and metaphysical roles. Guided by traditional master builders (undagi), serpent motifs anchor temple staircases, foundations, and royal baths, marking the threshold between the profane outer world and the sacred inner sanctuary. At water temples like Tirta Empul and Goa Gajah, serpentine sculptures guard water spouts and gates, channeling tirtha (holy water) to oversee both the physical purity of water and the metaphysical purification of the soul.

While rooted in Indian and Southeast Asian traditions, the Balinese Nāga is uniquely localized. Rather than focusing on destructive power, Balinese mythology reshapes the serpent into a emblem of balance and community guardianship. This reflects a synthesis with pre-Hindu animism—a heritage preserved in villages where offerings are still left at sacred trees and rivers.

This protective balance comes alive during religious observances like Odalan (temple anniversaries) and Melasti (ocean purification), where Nāga effigies are paraded to the sea to cleanse the community and bridge the seen world (sekala) with the unseen spiritual realm (niskala).

Today, the Nāga remains a central symbol across shadow puppetry (wayang kulit), performing arts, and ceremonial regalia. Even amidst modern tourism, the watchful Nāga stands as a timeless sentinel of Bali’s living spiritual foundations.

objects.title: Bencha for Water-Pouring Tradition
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
The Bencha is a small, tiered pavilion — a form of temporary architecture — used during the Songkran festival for bathing Buddha images and pouring water over the elderly. Songkran marks the vernal equinox and the end of the hot dry season, a period of new beginnings. The Bencha is distinguished by its stacked roof, intricate Kanok patterns (a flame-like or stylised leaf design)  and gold-leaf lacquer.

A key feature is the Naga-shaped water flume, which symbolises the Great Serpent spouting water as an offering to the Buddha and a prayer for abundance. Pouring water through this flume allows devotees to show respect without direct physical contact. The Naga's image here significant: as a creature whose nature is bound to water, it is a fitting vessel through which blessing flows — linking the mythological power of the serpent to the communal act of renewal.

This tradition also functions as a social glue, fostering unity through the collective construction of the pavilion, while reflecting gratitude toward elders and the belief that the power of water brings coolness and prosperity to the community.

objects.title: Embossed Brass Basin with Mythical Animal Motifs
objects.title_raw: Embossed Brass Basin with Mythical Animal Motifs
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This repoussé and chased brass holy water basin (khan nam mon) is a prime specimen of Southern Thai metal artistry, produced historically in the major coastal principalities (hua mueang) of Southern Thailand — most notably Nakhon Si Thammarat and Songkhla — which served as metallurgical hubs intertwined with maritime trading networks, fostering cultural exchanges between the Thai, Malay, and Chinese worlds.

The artistic composition of the basin is anchored by a structured layout of auspicious animals embossed around its body, featuring the Elephant (Chang), the Tiger (Suea), the Naga (Phaya Nak), the Rajasiha (Ratchasiha, the mythical lion), the Garuda (Khrut), and the Bear (Mee). Each carries symbolic weight rooted in regional folklore and cosmological thought: the Elephant represents physical strength, institutional stability, and agricultural fertility; the Naga, the element of water, rainmaking, and subterranean abundance; the Rajasiha, sovereign command and divine protection; and the Garuda, supreme authority and power over evil spirits. Consolidating this specific pantheon of beasts onto a single vessel reflects an ancient ideological pursuit: channelling the balancing forces of nature to manifest comprehensive good fortune. In folk theology, these animal motifs are linked to the concept of Guardian Spirits (Sat Phu Phitak); arranging such a diverse assembly around the basin acts as a metaphor for summoning spiritual energies from all directional axes into the ritual space.

The vessel was hand-shaped from a single piece of brass and embellished using the repoussé technique (dun lai noon tam): the metalsmith works from the reverse side, hammering the metal outward to create raised, three-dimensional designs, before flipping the vessel over to execute precision chasing from the front — a craft demanding intimate mastery of metallurgy and intense concentration. Due to the highly intricate, labour-intensive and costly production process, such basins were exclusively commissioned for prominent temples or held by wealthy merchants, community leaders, and the elite.

The holy water basin is used to contain consecrated holy water (nam phra phuttha mon) for protective chanting assemblies, ordinations, weddings, monastic bathing rites, and housewarming blessings.Within these settings, the water serves as a conductor of collective faith and divine blessings, and, in the context of Southern Thai society historically shaped by riverine ecosystems, as a sanctified symbol of purity, seasonal abundance, and communal nourishment.

Beyond ornament, the animals depicted on this basin — the elephant, naga, garuda, and mythical lion — represent a shared symbolic vocabulary that circulated across maritime Southeast Asia. Through the metalworking techniques that transformed these regional beliefs into a single crafted object, the basin reveals how knowledge, materials, and animal-inspired meanings travelled alongside the communities that shaped the region’s shared heritage.
