objects.title: Flintlock Firearm
objects.caption: These earrings originated in Indonesia and have traditionally been worn by Balinese and Javanese women during ceremonies and other important occasions. Their design draws inspiration from the naga, the mythical serpent, whose associations with protection, wisdom, and prosperity have long been expressed through Southeast Asia's artistic traditions. Finely crafted in gold, the earrings reflect the enduring place of the naga in Indonesian jewellery and ceremonial dress

objects.title: Langguai with Frog and Snake Motifs
objects.title_raw: Langguai with Frog and Snake Motifs
objects.caption:
This brass langguai is a traditional Malay container used to store the ingredients required for betel chewing. Brass and copper craftsmanship had been well established during this period, particularly in Kampong Ayer, which was renowned for its metalworking tradition.

The main compartment held betel leaves, while smaller compartments (anak-anak langguai) placed on the lid stored lime, gambir, and areca nut. Produced in various sizes, langguai served multiple functions: while smaller examples were used for everyday betel preparation, larger forms could also store garments, valuables, and, at times, food such as meat. In both domestic and ceremonial contexts, elaborately crafted langguai were objects of display, presented when receiving honoured guests or during important occasions. Historically, finely made examples also formed part of royal regalia and the possessions of elite households.

This example is distinguished by its engraved decoration, including a coiling snake and frogs that encircles the body alongside floral motifs. Such designs were not merely ornamental. The snake on this langguai therefore connected domestic hospitality with a wider world of prestige and symbolism. As betel culture travelled across maritime Southeast Asia, so too did the visual languages attached to the vessels that carried it. The snake’s presence on a Bruneian betel container demonstrates how a shared symbol of power was locally reinterpreted. It linked the refinement of the household to the broader cultural networks of Southeast Asia.

The craftsmanship of the langguai further reinforced its status. Brunei became particularly known for its brass langguai, with artisans producing elaborate forms decorated according to the preferences of their buyers. Motifs could include floral patterns, geometric designs, and animal imagery such as lizards, dragons, and snakes, reflecting a wider regional tradition in which skilled metalwork and auspicious symbols elevated functional objects into expressions of identity and standing

objects.title: Naga Motifs on a Kolek Boat in the style of Southern Thailand
objects.title_raw: Naga Motifs on a Kolek Boat in the style of Southern Thailand
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
The kolek is a traditional fishing vessel of the Lower South of Thailand. Known also as the buatan barat across the border in Northern Malaysia, its hulls are carved and painted with motifs draw together Thai, Malay, and Javanese traditions. The kolek's builders work without lofting or drafting techniques; the design emerges instead from the builder's imagination and experience, shaped by the owner's requirements for size and materials. Each boat is, in this sense, an unrepeatable object.

The hulls often feature images of the Naga, Hanuman, and the Burong Singo (Lion-Bird), amidst waves and floral vines. Featured on this boat, the Naga, specifically, represents authority, abundance, and protection from the sea. Alongside the bright colours, its presence is intended to project bravery and fierceness — qualities a vessel and its crew would need on open water. These designs are therefore not just artistic; they are spiritual anchors for fishermen, reflecting a worldview that sees the ocean as both a source of life and a sacred space.

The kolek and its imagery belong to a region whose cultural geography long preceded the borders that now divide it. As far back as the second century AD, ancient settlements here linked the markets of India and China across a shared trans-Peninsular route. Though the arrival of Islam and Theravada Buddhism drew this area into two distinct cultural orbits, they continued to share natural resources, agricultural and trading life, and a common material culture. The region was also situated between two overlapping centres of power — the Thai mandala radiating from the Chao Phraya delta, and the Malay mandala of the Melaka and Johor empires.

The kolek, still in use among fishermen in Kelantan and Pattani today, is thus an artifact of these layered relationships: a vessel whose painted Naga speaks not to one tradition but to the intertwined cosmologies of a shared sea.

objects.title: Naga-Headed Walking Stick
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This walking stick is carved from wood, its curved handle topped with the open-mouthed head of a serpent (Naga). The carving of scales runs down the handle and into the shaft of the stick itself, and in this manner the serpent’s body becomes the object in its entirety.

Thailand has long drawn on multiple calendrical traditions, including the Chinese lunar calendar and its zodiac, which is used to mark stages of life and key transitions. When this system was adopted into Thai culture, its twelve-year cycle was preserved, with certain adaptations -- notably, the Chinese dragon was reinterpreted through the image of the Naga, a figure deeply rooted in regional belief. In the Southern Thai way of life, the Naga is not merely a creature of legend but a symbol linking the power of water, the cosmos, and human destiny. Because of this cultural significance, the Naga was incorporated into the zodiac as the equivalent of the Year of the Dragon (Great Snake), signifying prestige and protection.

This object therefore demonstrates the woodworker's skill and the integration of cyclical time into daily life, where the Naga acts as a guardian of one's fate and a harbinger of auspiciousness.

objects.title: Naga-Shaped Carved Wooden Corbel (Khantruay)
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
The belief in the Naga as a guardian of sacred spaces is evident in carved wooden corbels (Khantruay) such as this one. These elements support the eaves of religious buildings and carry profound symbolic weight. Southern Thai craftsmen traditionally adapt the Naga’s form into structures that are both sturdy and beautiful. They carve the serpent's body with graceful curves, blending detailed scales and flame-like patterns with the fluid aesthetics of Malay art.

The Naga’s role as protector can be traced to early societies on the Siam Peninsula, where serpent cults along the Mekong River revered it as a symbol of fertility, water, and nourishment. This association was reinforced in Buddhist tradition through the story of Mucalinda, the Naga king who sheltered the meditating Sakyamuni Buddha from a storm by coiling his body around him and spreading his hood overhead, further establishing the serpent as a guardian figure.

Nagas were therefore placed in key positions in temple architecture, appearing on finials, gable boards, arches, balustrades, roof tiers, and stairways leading to the main shrine. This architectural symbolism draws on Hindu-Buddhist cosmology, in which the temple represents Mount Meru, the sacred mountain at the centre of the universe. Naga imagery along the roof tiers evokes the cosmic river of life flowing from this mountain into the human world. In this light, the corbel gives physical form to cosmology, situating the building within a sacred geography.

The presence of the Naga in religious architecture is not unique to Thailand. Across Southeast Asia — in Myanmar, Malaysia, Indonesia, and beyond — it appears in both vernacular and sacred structures, a shared guardian figure whose recurring form reflects a regional tradition of invoking divine protection in the built environment.

objects.title: Statue of Shiva
objects.caption:
This gilt bronze statue of the Hindu god Shiva is frontal-facing, crowned, and dressed in full regalia. The broad shoulders and minimal articulation of musculature are characteristic of the Sukhothai style. His third eye appears as a vertical line on the forehead, and both hands are held in the katakahasta mudra, with the index and little fingers pointing upward, and the third and fourth fingers clasped over the palm, as the gesture of one holding a flower such as a lotus or lily. The regalia, signifying divine authority, is gilded throughout — including the Yajnopavita, the sacred thread that marks priestly status, slung across his chest over the left shoulder. From behind this thread, the head of a Naga emerges, gilt like the rest of his regalia.

The serpent, commonly worn by Shiva around his neck or as a Yajnopavita, and sometimes shown encircling his throat, symbolises the potent venom he consumed during the Samudra Manthana (Churning of the Ocean of Milk). To prevent the venom from devastating the world, Shiva held it in his throat; his consort, Parvati, fearing for his safety, constricted his neck to contain it. This mythic event is reflected in religious painting through the darkened hue of Shiva’s throat (Nilakantha), while in statuary, the venom is personified by the serpent. Here, the serpent serves as a testament to divine sacrifice and love.

Commercial links between the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia date from at least the second century BCE, with migrations across the Indian Ocean to South and Southeast Asia occurring from around 500 BC into the early centuries AD. By the fifth and sixth centuries, epigraphic records across Southeast Asia attest to the enactment of Brahmanical ritual for local rulers, as beliefs from the Indian subcontinent blended with existing animistic traditions to produce a hybridised religious culture that persists in Thailand even to the present day. Early Shiva statuary in Thailand dates to the 6th century AD. Though the main religion of the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms, like that of Thailand today, was Theravada Buddhism, Hindu gods such as Shiva occupied a position of honour as guardians of the state, regarded as powerful and worthy of homage by kings and communities alike.

The Naga coiled at Shiva's neck arrives in Thailand through this current of Hindu transmission, yet the serpent was already present in the region's cosmological imagination long before, rooted in traditions that predate the arrival of Brahmanical belief and that gave the Naga its power across Southeast Asia beyond the sole influence of any one religious system.

objects.title: "Gold Swan" Commemorative Fan for the Cremation of Mom Suphab Kridakorn Na Ayudhaya, a Wife of Prince Nares Varariddhi
objects.title_raw: "Gold Swan" Commemorative Fan for the Cremation of Mom  Suphab Kridakorn Na Ayudhaya, a Wife of Prince Nares Varariddhi
objects.caption:
This commemorative fan, designed by His Royal Highness Prince Narisara Nuwattiwong and bestowed upon Mom Chao Ithithepsan Kritdakorn for the funeral of Mom Suphap Kridakorn na Ayutthaya in 1925, takes the form of a phat na nang ceremonial fan.
Fashioned from pale greenish-white silk and embroidered with multicoloured threads, it depicts a hamsa standing upon an eight-pointed wooden pedestal, its long tail ending in eye-like motifs resembling the tail feathers of a peacock. The pedestal serves also as the base from which flowering phutthan vines spread and bloom around the hamsa; within the right floral panel, the symbol "น." appears enclosed within a heart motif.

The hamsa here is a tribute in animal form. It serves as a symbolic representation of the name "Suphap" and signifies nobility, elegance, and purity, qualities reflective of Mom Suphap's character. These qualities become even more emphasized in the image of a bird that embodies precisely those associations in Lanna and Buddhist traditions. The bird also alludes to Suphap’s Mon ancestry, as the hamsa is regarded as a sacred creature in Mon culture and is closely associated with Hongsawadi (Hanthawaddy), the former capital of the Mon kingdom.

Through a single waterbird, the fan preserves three aspects of the deceased’s identity: her name, the virtues attributed to her character, and her ancestral heritage. In this process, the hamsa serves as a visual language through which Thai courtly practice, Buddhist ideals, and Mon cultural memory are brought together in an act of remembrance.

objects.title: Bangau and Okok
objects.caption:
The Bangau is a wooden component perched at the bow of a fishing vessel, its "neck" extending gracefully over the port side. The Okok, often referred to as the Anak Bangau (Young Stork), is positioned on the starboard side as its companion. Fashioned from resilient hardwoods such as Cengal, Meranti, Jelutung, or Pulai, and ranging from 40 cm to 1 metre in height and width, these carvings serve physically to support the sails and act as cleats for anchor lines or nets.

These Buatan Barat vessels—also known as kolek or kolae—are commissioned by fishermen in Kelantan and Terengganu from master craftsmen in Southern Thailand, in the provinces of Pattani, Narathiwat, and Yala. They are celebrated for their vibrant palettes and intricate, symbolic carvings. The name Bangau is derived from the stork, a bird synonymous with patience and precision in the coastal marshes. Okok is believed to stem from the word Bongkok (hunched), or Ongkok in the local Terengganu dialect. The bird's stoic nature makes it a symbol of vigilance, resilience, and the successful gathering of sustenance (rezeki). In the lore of East Coast fishermen, the Bangau is believed to possess a Semangat (spirit) that guards the vessel in the open sea. A strict code of conduct—or Adab—surrounds these objects; for instance, crew members must never turn their backs to the Bangau while sailing, nor step over it carelessly. To violate these taboos is to risk the safety of the crew and the bounty of the catch.

The Bangau and Okok are mirrors of a shared Southeast Asian maritime legacy. The historical trade routes and the mobility of boat builders between Peninsular Malaysia and Southern Thailand created a cultural corridor that defies modern political borders. This tradition demonstrates how maritime communities across the region share a common visual language and a similar sea-bound cosmology. In the context of cultural heritage, the Bangau and Okok are tangible artifacts that carry a vast intangible weight. They encapsulate ancient craftsmanship, belief systems, and communal values. As a cornerstone of Southeast Asian heritage, they prove that art, spirituality, and economic life are inextricably intertwined in the region's maritime soul.

objects.title: Blue and White Dish with Flattened Foliate Rim, Decorated with a Pale Blue Scene Depicting a Crane Surrounded by Plants
objects.title_raw: Blue and White Dish with Flattened Foliate Rim, Decorated with  a Pale Blue Scene Depicting a Crane Surrounded by Plants
objects.caption:
This dish depicts a crane standing in a body of water, surrounded by plants with a decorative border around the rim. It was recovered from the Brunei Shipwreck discovered in 1997, 32 nautical miles off the coast of Brunei at a depth of 62 metres. The excavation uncovered more than 13,000 artefacts, the majority of which were ceramics dated to the late 15th to early 16th century AD.

Produced at the kilns of Jingdezhen in Jiangxi Province, China, this blue and white ware is characteristic of the Ming dynasty, a period regarded as a golden age for Chinese ceramics. At this time, a shift from stoneware to porcelain established the cobalt blue underglaze style as the most recognisable form of Chinese export ware. The kilns at Jingdezhen supplied both imperial wares and the vast international markets that carried Chinese ceramics across maritime Southeast Asia and beyond.

The crane on this dish carried its meaning with it. In Chinese culture, the crane represents longevity and good fortune, associations that made it a natural choice for objects intended to impress, to gift, and to circulate as markers of prestige. Recovered from the hold of a ship that never reached its destination, this dish demonstrates one way through which the crane motif moved through the maritime trade network which connected China to the ports of Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Celadon-Glazed Kendi in Goose Form
objects.collection: Brunei Darussalam Maritime Museum, Brunei Museum Department
objects.caption:
This ceramic ewer, modelled in the form of a hamsa bird — the Sanskrit word haṃsa (हंस) often translated as goose — is the only known hamsa-shaped ewer in the collection of the Maritime Museum of Brunei Darussalam. Kendi of this type were used for water-pouring ritual as well as for everyday functions, their zoomorphic forms a way of investing the daily act of pouring with the associations the animal carried. The hamsa, regarded as a symbol of purity and protection across Hindu-Buddhist traditions, ensured that water dispensed through this vessel arrived already charged with auspicious meaning.

Likely brought to the region through the Maritime Silk Road in the late 15th to early 16th century, this kendi reflects the movement of prestige goods that accompanied diplomatic missions and long-distance trade. Yet the hamsa-shaped kendi was also a domestic object, handled in everyday contexts, used to pour water at table and in ceremony alike. In this manner, the hamsa moved between sacred and domestic worlds, carrying with it meanings accumulated across the interconnected communities of maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Common Kingfisher
objects.caption:
As its name suggests, the common kingfisher (Alcedo atthis) is a bird renowned for its diving technique, which it uses to hunt for fish underwater. It also occasionally feeds on other creatures such as lizards, frogs and insects. This bird is small, just about 16 centimetres long, and it is easily recognisable from its vibrant turquoise blue and reddish-brown plumage. While this bird has a widespread breeding range across Eurasia and North Africa, some of its temperate-dwelling populations also migrate southwards during winter. In Singapore, this is the most common migratory kingfisher that can be encountered. It is often found near water bodies, such as ponds, rivers and mangroves.

In Malay, the kingfisher is known as burung pekaka, "pekaka" is derived from the bird's call. This possibly refers to other kingfisher species such as the collared kingfisher (Todiramphus chloris), whose call is a loud "keek-keek". In comparison, the common kingfisher's call is a high, shrill whistle. Given the shyness of this bird and its tendency to perch hidden among tree foliage, it is often more easy to spot it by following the sound of its call. Kingfishers are highly sensitive to the conditions of a freshwater ecosystem, as they rely on good water quality and an abundance of fish in order to hunt properly. As such, the presence of kingfishers is a good indicator of a healthy ecosystem.

Within regional indigenous beliefs, kingfishers are often regarded as guardians of the water. In Taal, the Philippines, the southern silvery kingfisher (locally known as kasay-kasay) also has religious associations, where they feature in a legend about the discovery of the Catholic image of Our Lady of Caysasay.

objects.title: Hamsa Bird Water Container
objects.caption:
This bronze hamsa has its head raised upward, its neck and wings decorated with kanok motifs and floral designs. Dating to the 16th–17th century, it is believed to have served as a vessel for containing consecrated water used in ritual ceremonies. King Rama VII received this object during his royal visit to Northern Thailand in 1926 and later bestowed it upon the museum.

In Lanna culture, the hamsa is regarded as a symbol of purity, making it an especially appropriate form for a vessel through which sacred water is poured during ceremonies. The bird also appears in other auspicious motifs, including the Purna-Ghata (Vase of Plenty), where it is associated with abundance and prosperity. Within Buddhist traditions, the hamsa is recognised as an auspicious symbol among the 108 signs of the Buddha and appears in numerous Jataka tales.

The hamsa’s significance, however, extends beyond Buddhism. In Hindu tradition, it is the mythical vehicle of the deity Brahma, and originates from the sacred realm of Mount Meru, the abode of the gods. Across Thailand, this sacred bird was incorporated into other ritual objects — often ones with close associations to water, too —  including hamsa-shaped kendi and water vessels in which the bird’s mouth served as a spout. The continued presence of the hamsa in Sukhothai-Sawankhalok and Lanna traditions reflects a period when Theravada Buddhism, Brahmanical practices, and animistic folk belief existed alongside and shaped one another. By taking the form of the hamsa, this ritual vessel thus imbues the consecrated water it holds with the qualities attributed to the bird — purity, auspiciousness, and spiritual merit.

The hamsa’s long symbolic history across Lanna, Buddhist, and wider Hindu-Buddhist traditions of South and Southeast Asia demonstrates how animal forms were repeatedly adapted into ritual practice. Although its meanings varied across communities, the waterbird consistently occupied a position between the earthly and sacred realms, transformed here into the very vessel through which blessings were transmitted.

objects.title: Keris Pekaka
objects.caption:
This keris originates from Kelantan and features a wooden hilt carved in the likeness of a Javanese shadow puppet character. It is known as Keris Pekaka due to its long, silver-covered tip that resembles the beak of a kingfisher bird (burung pekaka). The sheath is made of glossy kemuning wood, highlighting its natural beauty. The upper part of the sheath (sampir) curves gracefully with a long, straight blade, reflecting the fine craftsmanship of Kelantanese artisans. All the same, the shadow puppet-like carving on the hilt embeds the performative traditions of the Malay Peninsula into an object carried as a marker of prestige.

The keris is unique to island Southeast Asia and is one of the most significant objects of material culture across communities from Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula to Java, Borneo, Sulawesi, Mindanao, and Sumbawa. The keris occupied multiple roles in Malay societies: as a weapon, heirloom, ceremonial object, and visible expression of status and identity. Its value lay not only in its function, but in the craftsmanship, materials, and meanings accumulated around it. In the Keris Pekaka, the kingfisher’s distinctive beak is transformed into a symbol of refinement, giving the weapon a connection to the natural world while distinguishing it as an object of artistic and social importance.

Keris of this type are also found in Pattani, Southern Thailand. They reflect centuries of movement between Kelantan and Pattani through trade, shared courtly traditions, and the circulation of artisans and artistic styles. The presence of the same keris forms across the modern border points to a time when Kelantan and Pattani belonged to a connected cultural sphere. Back then prestige was expressed through shared forms of craftsmanship, courtly taste, and symbolic imagery drawn from the natural world.

objects.title: Offering Vessel (Hsun Ok) in the Form of a Hinta Bird
objects.title_raw: Offering Vessel (Hsun Ok) in the Form of a Hinta Bird
objects.caption:
This rare, bird-shaped offering vessel (Hsun Ok) demonstrates the technical mastery of Burmese lacquer makers. A lacquer putty mixture called thayo — literally "flesh and bones" — was freely modelled or moulded, stuck onto the surface, and embellished with gold leaf. Inlaid semi-precious stones, glass, and mirror pieces add further value. The result is an object that deploys the full vocabulary of Burmese applied lacquer to give form to one of the most sacred birds in Mon culture.

The term hintha derives from the Pali and Sanskrit word haṁsa, which refers both to mythical birds and real waterfowl such as swans and geese. In Mon tradition, however, the hintha developed into a distinctive sacred bird associated with the origins of their homeland. According to Mon legend, when the Buddha travelled and preached in the region, he encountered a pair of hinthas resting on a small piece of dry land surrounded by water. The Buddha foretold that this place would one day become a prosperous city where his teachings would flourish. In 514 CE, the city of Hanthawaddy (present-day Bago) was established on this site, preserving the memory of the prophecy through its name, meaning “city of the hintha”. Another version of the legend recounts that the land was so small that only one bird could stand upon it, causing the female hintha to rest on the back of the male. This image of paired hinthas became a recurring motif in Mon religious art, royal objects such as betel boxes, shoes, and thrones, as well as everyday objects.

Its significance was further reinforced through Buddhist literature, particularly the Javana Hamsa Jataka, in which the Buddha was said to have been a king of the hinthas in a previous life. In this tale, the hintha king teaches a human ruler that the passing of time and the inevitability of death are greater than any worldly achievement, encouraging him to practise the virtues expected of a righteous king. Because of this association with wisdom and moral instruction, hintha figures were placed atop prayer posts in temples throughout Myanmar.

As a Hsun Ok, or Buddhist offering vessel, this object brings these layers of meaning into devotional practice. Food presented through the image of the sacred bird becomes connected to Mon origin traditions, Buddhist teachings, and the auspicious qualities attributed to the creature.

The presence of sacred swans in the material cultures of Myanmar, Thailand, and neighbouring regions reflects the movement of animal symbolism and Buddhist traditions across mainland Southeast Asia. Yet its meaning remained rooted in local histories. For the Mon, the waterbird became a marker of sacred geography and collective identity, and for Buddhist communities, it embodied wisdom, generosity, and spiritual aspiration.

objects.title: Đông Sơn Drum
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This bronze drum, found in Nakhon Si Thammarat province, was used for requesting rain. Its drumhead is decorated with a 12-pointed star, geometric patterns arranged within concentric circles, and a counter-clockwise flying bird motif of a kind of egret — a waterbird whose natural domain spans the sky and the water below, making it a fitting presence on an instrument believed to call rain from one into the other. A pair of cast-in ears are attached to the sides above the drum body.

This style of drum is commonly found during the bronze age of Thailand, and is related to the Dong Son culture, a metal age culture of Vietnam dating back approximately 2700 years. Created through the lost-wax casting method, such drums were objects of considerable technical skill and were often found in elite or ceremonial contexts, including burials and ritual spaces. Their sounds were believed to summon rain, encourage agricultural fertility, protect communities, and bring people together for ancestral ceremonies. Possessing and using such drums also expressed the authority of community leaders who mediated these relationships between people, ancestors, and the natural world.

The egret and other waterbirds were intimately connected to the seasonal rhythms of water, rain, and agricultural abundance across early Southeast Asian communities. Depicted circling the starburst centre of the drum, the waterbird reflects a worldview in which creatures of the air and water participated in maintaining cosmic balance and agricultural prosperity. The presence of this motif on a bronze drum found in southern Thailand also points to a wider regional connection. Through networks linking ancient communities across mainland Southeast Asia, both metalworking techniques, as well as shared understandings of the natural and spiritual worlds, travelled together.

objects.title: Estuarine Crocodile
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum
objects.caption:
Found along the coasts, estuaries and rivers of Southeast Asia, Crocodylus porosus, the estuarine crocodile is the largest living reptile in the world. It can still be seen in Singapore's waters today, and while these creatures are considered dangerous, their presence as apex predators (occupying the top of the food chain) often indicates that an ecosystem is healthy and stable.

This particular crocodile was donated to the Raffles Museum in September 1887, making it one of the oldest heritage specimens in our collections today. It was a wild crocodile that had been shot on the bank of the Serangoon River that same year by George Paddison Owen, a Eurasian resident known locally for his recreational hunting exploits. The specimen was subsequently preserved by the Raffles Museum's taxidermist of the time, L.A. Fernandis.

More than just a specimen, this crocodile also had links to regional spiritual worlds, specifically relating to notions of the keramat, which are sacred shrine sites that can typically be found in Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Within the varied historical accounts of a keramat in Butterworth, Malaysia, known as 'Meriam Timbul' or 'Floating Cannon Shrine', one story suggests that the cannon—which worshippers would make offerings to for good luck—belonged to "Panglima" (Warrior) Ah Chong, who turned into a crocodile on his death. It was speculated that this was the very crocodile that was shot and donated to the Raffles Museum in 1887.

While it is difficult to verify the accuracy of this conjecture, crocodiles and keramats were consistently associated, and even a living crocodile could be a sacred guardian of a place. In the 1960s in Singapore, a 6-metre long crocodile living in Sungei Katransdut was regarded by residents and fishermen in the area as a protector—and they believed that if the crocodile came to any harm, the fishermen would not be able to live along the river any longer.

In earlier regional histories, the buaya putih ("white crocodile" in Malay) is also a mythical figure that has appeared in various stories. One tale is found in the Hikayat Hang Tuah, which chronicles the life of a Malay warrior Hang Tuah who lived in the Sultanate of Malacca in the 15th century. In this episode, the Raja of Malacca was sailing through the Singapore Straits when his crown dropped into the sea. Only Hang Tuah had the courage to jump into the water to retrieve the crown—but just as he was about to succeed, a white crocodile appeared and bit down on his keris, a traditional dagger that also holds important spiritual significance. In a drawn-out duel with the crocodile, Hang Tuah lost his keris despite holding on to the raja'scrown. As such, the white crocodile was regarded as a bad omen—a warning for the raja to stay away and return home.

Today in Malaysia, Hang Tuah still has some association with the white crocodile: an urban legend states that Hang Tuah's Well, located in Malacca, houses a white crocodile that can only be seen by worthy religious scholars. Beyond the role of spiritual protectors and guardians, crocodiles are also regular characters that appear in regional myths and tales. Most prominently, the island of Timor—which today is divided between Timor-Leste and Indonesia—is said to have been formed from the body of a crocodile. The creature also features in various folktales across Southeast Asia, perhaps the most well-known trope being that of a small animal outwitting crocodiles to cross the river. In some tellings of this story, the trickster animal is a mousedeer, while other versions involve a monkey or rabbit.

objects.title: Makara Palanquin Ornament
objects.caption:
The makara is a composite mythical creature with features drawn from animals of both land and water, including the crocodile, fish, goat, and elephant. In Hindu tradition, it serves as the vehicle of the river goddess Ganga, and its ability to move across different realms reflects its association with water, fertility, and the life-giving forces of nature. As a mythical creature originating in early Indian traditions, the makara travelled across the Indian Ocean and became embedded in the artistic and ceremonial traditions of Hindu-Buddhist societies throughout South and Southeast Asia.

This rare surviving makara ornament once formed part of a palanquin from the Malay Peninsula, likely produced in Pattani in the 18th or 19th century. Although originating from Hindu-Buddhist visual traditions, the makara remained meaningful within Muslim Malay communities of the northeastern Malay Peninsula, where it continued to be understood as a protective water spirit and a symbol of fertility and abundance.

The palanquin was used in village ceremonies associated with the circumcision of young boys — a rite of passage required by Islamic practice but deeply shaped by local customs. During these celebrations, circumcised boys were paraded and presented to the wider community, marking their transition into a new stage of social and religious life. The presence of the makara on such a ceremonial object demonstrates how older regional symbols were reinterpreted within new religious contexts.

Through this object, the makara reveals a broader Southeast Asian pattern. Royal and communal traditions often preserved and transformed visual languages across changing religious landscapes. A creature born from Hindu-Buddhist cosmology became, in a Malay Muslim setting, a guardian of ceremony, continuity, and community identity.

objects.title: Antique Chinese Blue and White Porcelain Pillow
objects.title_raw: Antique Chinese Blue and White Porcelain Pillow
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This Chinese porcelain pillow is formed from dense high-fired stoneware, coated with a smooth white glaze, and decorated with underglaze cobalt blue painting. Its compact rectangular form and cool-to-the-touch surface reflect the practical design of ceramic pillows, a tradition of Chinese household objects that travelled through trade and migration to communities across Southeast Asia, including Sino-Thai families in Southern Thailand.

The pillow’s cooling quality was central to its use. High-fired glazed ceramic naturally dissipates body heat, helping to keep the sleeper’s head and neck cool in accordance with traditional Chinese medical principles. The latter emphasised maintaining a cool head and warm feet for bodily balance. Its firm elevation also provided support for the neck during rest. Similar ceramic pillows were used by physicians as wrist supports when taking a patient’s pulse.

The pillow’s decoration transformed this practical object into one of protection and blessing. The central panel depicts a pair of mythical guardian lions playing with a sacred ribboned ball, their manes and tails rendered in flowing lines that echo traditional Chinese flame motifs. The surrounding borders feature continuous scrollwork associated with uninterrupted continuity and lasting fortune. In Chinese visual traditions, guardian lions were protectors capable of warding off harmful forces and safeguarding the household, while the sacred ball symbolised wisdom, completeness, and success. Together, the pair expressed wishes for peace, prosperity, and protection, particularly fitting for an object placed beside the body during sleep.

Ceramic pillows were also associated with important life transitions. From the Song through Ming periods, they were recorded as wedding gifts that conveyed wishes for harmony, longevity, and a stable family life. The guardian lions therefore gave symbolic meaning to an object already connected to bodily care: while the ceramic surface supported physical well-being, the animal imagery provided spiritual protection.

By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, porcelain pillows formed part of the material culture of Chinese communities in Southern Thailand, brought by Hokkien, Teochew, and Hakka migrants through expanding regional trade networks. Their presence reflects the movement not only of ceramics, but also of household practices and healing traditions across maritime Southeast Asia. In this context, the guardian lion on this pillow reinforces this connection between body and belief, in which the ceramic form cared for physical well-being, while the protective animal imagery offered spiritual safeguarding.

objects.title: Balinese Singha
objects.caption:
The lion (singa) does not exist in Southeast Asia, yet it has acquired a powerful presence in the region’s religious and artistic traditions. Through the spread of Hindu-Buddhist ideas, the lion came to represent sovereignty, protection, and sacred power. In Bali, this symbolic creature developed into the singa, a guardian figure that stands between the human and spirit worlds.

The most famous expression of the Balinese singa is the Barong Ket, the lion-like protector who battles the witch Rangda in ritual performances. Their eternal struggle represents the tension between opposing forces: chaos and order, destruction and protection. Rather than eliminating darkness, the performance renews the balance that allows the world to continue, reaffirming the Balinese belief that harmony depends on maintaining equilibrium between these forces.

These wooden figures from the Ada Guna Museum represent another expression of this tradition. Known as a singa bersayap (“winged lion”) or singa ambara raja (“lion king of the sky”), such figures adorned Balinese temples and palace complexes, placed above entrances, beneath roof structures, or used as sacred mounts for divine images during ritual processions. Its fierce expression, open jaws, bulging eyes, and extended wings communicate its role as a supernatural guardian. The wings, recalling the Garuda, further transform the lion from an earthly creature into a celestial being.

Although lions were never native to Bali, the singa became deeply embedded within Balinese Hindu culture through older Indian and Hindu-Buddhist traditions, where the lion represented kingship, divine authority, and protection. In sacred architecture, the semi-mythical form of the singa figures reinforced the temple as a protected cosmic space, with the temple itself understood as a symbolic reflection of Mount Meru, the sacred mountain at the centre of the universe in Hindu-Buddhist cosmology. Through these guardian figures, architectural spaces were connected to the divine order they represented.

Across Southeast Asia, the lion was similarly adapted into local traditions. In Myanmar, the lion became the chinthe, a guardian figure placed at the entrances of pagodas and important buildings. One legend tells of Sīhabāhu, the son of a lion and a human princess, who later killed his lion father and became king. To honour his father, he commissioned lion images for pagodas, giving the chinthe its associations with royal authority, protection, and Buddhist devotion.

In the Malay world, the lion entered local memory through the founding legend of Singapore. According to tradition, the Sumatran prince Sri Tri Buana (Sang Nila Utama) encountered a powerful animal at Temasek believed to be a lion and named the settlement Singapura, from the Sanskrit singa (“lion”) and pura (“city”).

The Balinese singa, Burmese chinthe, and Malay singa demonstrate how an animal absent from Southeast Asia’s natural landscape became deeply rooted in its cultural memory. Carried through shared religious traditions and reshaped through local myths, rituals, and political histories, the lion was transformed from a distant symbol into a guardian figure made meaningful by each community.

objects.title: Gold-Sheathed Lion-Shaped Betel Nut Cutter
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This betel nut cutter from Yala Province is forged from high-grade steel and entirely sheathed in gold. Its pivot head, the functional joint that opens and closes the cutter, is sculpted as a lion (Singha), with expressive eyes, sharp fangs, and a flowing mane conveying strength and protection. The gold sheathing extends along both handles, culminating in delicate granulation work depicting budding lotuses, a motif associated with purity and the flourishing of Buddhist teachings.

Across Southeast Asia, betel cutters were used to prepare areca nuts for chewing with betel leaves, lime, and aromatic spices. This example belonged to a more ceremonial context. Gold-sheathed betel sets (Chian Mak) were associated with royalty, high-ranking officials, wealthy merchants, and senior Buddhist clergy. In the Rattanakosin period, royal records describe such sets being presented to senior monks according to their rank, showing how betel objects could also express social and religious status.

The lion and lotus were carefully chosen symbols. Across Hindu-Buddhist traditions, the Singha came to represent courage, protection, and authority, while the lotus symbolised purity and spiritual virtue. Together, they transformed an everyday implement into an object that communicated both social standing and religious meaning.

Found in Yala Province, this betel cutter also reflects the cultural exchanges that shaped the region. Here, Malay Muslim communities, Theravada Buddhist communities, and the Siamese court encountered one another, and symbols travelled across religious and cultural boundaries. The lion's enduring appeal lay in its ability to be understood in different contexts. Through its craftsmanship, materials, and imagery, this object reveals how shared symbols were continually adapted and reinterpreted by the communities who used them.

objects.title: Monk’s Alms Bowl
objects.caption:
This lacquered wood alms bowl, inlaid with mother-of-pearl, is decorated with the animals of the Chinese zodiac set amidst floral vegetation. The lid bears a large Buddhist lion, and the base carries the mark of a crown — details that together suggest this bowl was intended for a monk of aristocratic standing. It transforms a conventionally austere monastic object into a vessel of considerable prestige.

Mother-of-pearl, the iridescent inner lining of marine mollusc shells, was widely traded across the region. In Thailand, opalescent shells were used as early as the Dvaravati period (9th century) for architectural decoration. It became prominent during the Ayutthaya period when laws decreed it to be exclusively used for royal utensils; a department for the production of mother-of-pearl work was thus set up. These associations with the royal court and specialised craftsmanship gave mother-of-pearl objects a heightened prestige. As a result, the material became especially appropriate for acts of Buddhist merit-making: patrons offered elaborately crafted monastic objects, such as alms bowls, as valuable donations through which devotion and religious virtue could be expressed.

Reportedly found in Thailand and dating to the late 19th or early 20th century, this bowl reflects the circulation of mother-of-pearl craftsmanship and Buddhist devotional practices across mainland Southeast Asia. A material formed within the shells of marine creatures was transformed through human skill and religious intention into an object whose value lay not only in its beauty, but in its ability to embody generosity, devotion, and the pursuit of merit.
