objects.title: Singabarong Cloth
objects.caption:
This early 20th-century cotton cloth from West Java, features the Singa Barong, a sacred hybrid creature developed within the artistic traditions of the Cirebon Sultanate. The motif appeared in palace ceremonies, ritual performances, and courtly arts, reflecting the region’s history as a meeting point of different cultural influences.

Derived from the Sanskrit simha (“lion”), the Singa Barong combines the lion’s associations with courage, authority, and guardianship with elements drawn from other traditions. Its form brings together the Chinese dragon (naga), the Indian elephant (gajah), and the Islamic steed (buraq) in a creature of Javanese visual culture. As a sacred protective figure, it represented royal power and the ability to guard important thresholds between the human and spiritual worlds.

Although lions were not native to Java, the Singa Barong reveals how animal imagery travelled across Asia and was transformed through local traditions. The lion became not a foreign creature, but a powerful symbol through which Cirebon communities expressed authority, protection, and their place within wider networks of cultural exchange.

Key Reference: Aribowo, Widodo, and Khairul Mustaqim. "The Lion That Never Lived: Global Gestalt and Hermeneutic Reading of the Singa Barong Ornament in the Javanese Keris." SAP Community and Interculturality in Dialogue 5 (2025): 166-166.

objects.title: Bronze Drum / Đông Sơn Drum (Heger I)
objects.title_raw: Bronze Drum / Đông Sơn Drum (Heger I)
objects.caption:
This bronze drum was made in sections using the lost-wax casting method, topped by a bronze tympanum. At the centre of the tympanum is a starburst motif, circumscribed by concentric bands. These registers contain geometric designs as well as human figures engaging in daily life and ritual, birds, animals, and architecture. At the rim of the tympanum, four small high-relief figurines of rounded shells are evenly spaced, as if circumambulating the drum's edge.

Dong Son drums are known to sometimes feature small three-dimensional animal figures— most commonly frogs — placed at the rim in groups of four. This recurring configuration has been associated with seasonal cycles, rain-calling rituals, and the agricultural calendar. The shells on this drum may operate within a related symbolic framework. Their placement at the perimeter evokes the importance of water to the communities that produced and used these objects.

Dong Son drums were found primarily in elite or ceremonial contexts, such as private homes and in burials, suggesting they played a significant role in Bronze Age life across Southeast Asia. Their likely use spanned ritual, social, and symbolic purposes, including rain-making ceremonies, agricultural rites, and ancestral worship. Their sound was believed to call for fertility, protect the community, and gather people. The drums also symbolized the power and status of community leaders.

The earliest examples of such drums date from the late fourth century BCE in present-day northern Vietnam, where they were used for burial and funerary rites. Their subsequent distribution across the region reflects the Dong Son culture’s participation in extensive exchange networks. Drums have been discovered along major river systems, including the Red River in northern Vietnam and the Mekong, from Yunnan through Laos to Cambodia, as well as across maritime routes extending as far as Timor-Leste.

In the contemporaneous Dian culture of Yunnan’s lacustrine basins — a culture that likely shared reciprocal influences with Dong Son and imported its bronze drums — similar drums were repurposed as containers for storing cowries or marine shells that may have functioned as a form of currency in the region. This reuse suggests that shells held layered significance across early Southeast Asia: not only as markers of aquatic environments, but also as emblems of the networks of exchange, value, and influence linking coastal and inland worlds.

objects.title: Chanap
objects.caption:
A Chanap is a ritual offering used in prayers within Peranakan Chinese households. Made from preserved half-ripe papaya, the Chanap is intricately woven and carved into motifs such as crabs and flowers, and placed on a decorative box. Chanap is offered during major rituals and life events, including Lunar New Year, prayers to the Jade Emperor (Pai Thi Kong), weddings, and funerals. Often the most visually striking object on the altar, it forms the centre of the offering display.

The term is uniquely recognised by the Peranakan Chinese of Malacca and Singapore. Similar offerings in Penang, Phuket, and Indonesia are known as Bit Chien or Cien Nap/Hap, names that may derive from the Hokkien Chien Hap, meaning “sweet-preserves box”. The presence of closely related ritual forms across these port communities reflects the movement of Peranakan Chinese traditions through the maritime networks of Southeast Asia. Here shared practices developed alongside long histories of migration, trade, and settlement.

The papaya is traditionally carved into a crab, as the Chinese word for crab (xie) sounds like "harmony”, making the creature an auspicious symbol within the offering. By transforming a coastal animal into a ritual form, the Chanap brings together the natural resources of the region’s environments with the linguistic symbolism of Chinese tradition. It embeds wishes for harmony and prosperity into an everyday food material.

objects.title: Containers with Mother-of-Pearl Inlay
objects.caption:
These two “tiab” containers, each consisting of a tray supporting a cone-shaped cover, are inlaid with mother-of-pearl against a black lacquer ground. The left carries a layered four-petalled floral design with sprays of foliage, while the right features a lion set within a rice ball motif surrounded by stylised scrollwork. Used for presenting food to monks during royal ceremonies, they demonstrate how a material drawn from the sea was transformed into an object of courtly refinement.

Mother-of-pearl inlay, known to Thai craftsmen as khruang pradab muk, was among the most technically demanding of traditional crafts. Glossy, iridescent shells sourced from Thailand’s coastal provinces were cut into small pieces and then carefully set into a black lacquer surface by specialist craftsmen. The precision required in preparing, arranging, and polishing each fragment made mother-of-pearl work a highly valued craft associated with royal and religious institutions. During the Ayutthaya period, royal patronage further elevated the status of the craft, with formal regulations governing the ranks and lands of artisans involved in its production.

Mother-of-pearl was applied to objects of distinction including royal furniture, ordination hall doors, Buddhist manuscript cabinets, and ceremonial vessels. In these tiab containers, the rarity of the marine material and the skill required to transform it into intricate designs combined to create an object suited to the highest levels of ceremonial use. The shell’s natural brilliance, refined through human craftsmanship, and supported by royal patronage, became a visible expression of prestige in Siamese court culture.

The elevation of the shell from marine resource to courtly ornament reflects a wider Southeast Asian pattern in which the natural environment provided not only materials for survival, but also the resources through which societies expressed status and power.

objects.title: Cowrie Shells
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
Cowrie shells are the exoskeletons of small marine gastropods belonging to the family Cypraeidae. Characterised by their smooth, glossy texture, oval seed-like profiles, and varying natural hues ranging from porcelain white and cream to pale yellow and deep brown, these shells served as a highly efficient medium of exchange. Across historical markets in Southeast Asia, including the Southern Thai Peninsula, varieties such as Bia Chan, Bia Nang, and Bia Mu were valued for their consistent size, durability, and difficulty to imitate. Here, the cowrie shells are displayed alongside their metal replicas (Bia Loha).

Cowries were used in everyday transactions, from purchasing food and household goods to trading regional commodities and paying taxes. Even during the reigns of King Rama IV and King Rama V, when modern minted coinage was widely introduced by the central government, cowries remained a crucial currency for local trade within rural coastal communities. Whenever natural cowrie stocks became scarce, local authorities or merchant guilds produced Bia Loha — small cast metal replicas shaped specifically to mimic cowrie shells — marking the transition from natural currency to human-made token coinage. Their role in economic life is recorded in sources including the Law of the Three Seals (Kotmai Tra Sam Duang), royal administrative records, and regional literature.

The importance of cowries was closely tied to the environments that produced them. A local legend from Pak Phanang District, the Bia Sat (Washed-Up Cowrie) Legend, recounts historical periods when massive ocean swells deposited vast quantities of cowries onto the shoreline, allowing coastal villagers to gather them freely for use as currency. The story reflects the close relationship between coastal communities and the sea, while explaining the economic importance of the Pak Phanang estuary. The legacy of cowries remains embedded in language -- the word Bia continues to serve as the root term for financial concepts in everyday Thai, from Bia Liang (an allowance or stipend) to Bia Wat (a military pension).

Beyond exchange, cowries also acquired social and spiritual meanings. They were frequently used as convenient tokens and betting chips in traditional gambling games such as Ka Thua. In addition, their associations with good fortune, wealth, and maritime fertility led them to be incorporatedinto rituals and protective objects. In Southern Thai and Sino-Thai traditions, Bia Kae amulets made from cowrie shells were believed to protect against malevolent spirits, black magic, and misfortune, while shells buried beneath house foundations or sacred structures symbolised enduring prosperity. Ceremonial cowrie strands (Phuang Hoi Bia) were likewise used in votive offerings, the fulfillment of spiritual vows, and communal prayers for agricultural and oceanic abundance.

objects.title: Giant Clams
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chain Natural History Museum
objects.caption:
The giant clam (subfamily Tridacninae) is a magnificent marine bivalve deeply intertwined with both the delicate marine ecosystems and the rich cultural histories of Southeast Asia. Thriving in the shallow, clear waters of intertidal zones and coral reefs across the wider Indo-Pacific, these extraordinary creatures find a true sanctuary in Southeast Asia, which is home to eight of the world’s twelve giant clam species. In Thai waters alone, five species occur, with a remarkably dense concentration inhabiting the shallow reefs surrounding Koh Khai in Chumphon. Among these is the iconic Fluted Giant Clam, easily recognized on the reef by its long, heavy calcium carbonate shell featuring prominent, protruding scales known as scutes. Nestled within these hard walls is a fleshy, vibrant mantle that displays rich hues of purple, green, and yellow. These striking colors are produced by symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae, which live inside the tissue and provide the clam with essential nutrients through photosynthesis. In return for this solar-powered energy, the giant clams serve as highly efficient filter feeders, playing a vital role in keeping marine ecosystems healthy by removing excess nutrients from the water.

Beyond their ecological importance, giant clams hold profound historical and cultural significance in the region, reflecting a relationship with human communities that stretches back millennia. In Thailand, archaeological digs at the Bronze Age site of Ban Nam Daeng in Kanchanaburi Province have unearthed prehistoric tools and beautiful giant clam shell bracelets dating back some 3,500 to 4,000 years. The presence of these shell objects in areas far beyond the coast highlights early trade networks, suggesting that these durable marine materials circulated early as markers of exchange and social status. These shell forms naturally entered the visual cultures of the region; spiral motifs echoing snail shells appeared on pottery from 300 BC to 200 AD, and shell decorations on the Mahorathuek drum symbolized abundance and rain in agricultural societies. Even regional language preserves these maritime connections. In Thai, the word hoi (หอย), the general term for shellfish, is believed to trace back to the Cantonese hoi (ฮ่อย), meaning "sea"—a linguistic inheritance reflecting a long entanglement with seafaring cultures. While local folklore sometimes colorfully misportrayed these gentle giants as "killer clams," their beautiful shells were historically prized as religious objects, domestic basins, and exported ornaments. In Singapore, archaeological evidence underscores this long-standing presence, with tridacnid shells excavated near St Andrew’s Cathedral dating back approximately 500 years, and early museum collections securing local specimens as early as 1933.

Today, these living artifacts face unprecedented modern pressures that threaten their survival. Because giant clams are slow-growing and remain permanently anchored to fixed locations, recovering from drastic population declines is exceptionally difficult. Their shallow reef habitats make them highly vulnerable to coastal development, land reclamation, habitat degradation, and direct collection, with smaller clams frequently harvested for the international marine aquarium trade. In Singapore's coastal waters, where they were once abundant, populations have been severely depleted since the 1960s, driving several related species to local extinction and leaving the Fluted Giant Clam listed as Critically Endangered in the Singapore Red Data Book. Globally, the subfamily is listed as Conservation Dependent on the IUCN Red List and strictly protected under CITES regulations. Although international laws prohibit the illegal collection and trade of threatened giant clams, overharvesting continues in parts of the region, causing some species to disappear entirely from certain areas. Safeguarding reef habitats and water quality remains absolutely essential for their survival. In a determined effort to save and propagate these vital creatures, Thailand has pioneered successful marine conservation programs, successfully breeding and raising all of its native giant clam species to restore and repopulate the region's reefs.

objects.title: Kalung
objects.caption:
The Tanimbar Islands of Maluku have long been shaped by maritime life, and seashells remain an important part of the region's material culture. This traditional necklace, made from strands of cowrie shells, is worn by Tanimbar men, particularly customary elders, together with earrings and a woven headcloth.

Beyond its decorative function, the necklace signifies bravery, courage, strength, social status, wealth, and enduring connections with ancestors. Through objects such as this, cowrie shells became part of the visual language through which Tanimbar communities expressed identity, authority, and belonging.

objects.title: Mother of Pearl Furniture Depicting Animals
objects.title_raw: Mother of Pearl Furniture Depicting Animals
objects.caption:
This table and set of stools, made from ebony wood and inlaid with handcrafted mother-of-pearl in Guangdong province in the 18th century, represent a prestigious category of domestic furnishing in affluent Peranakan Chinese (Baba & Nyonya) homes. Intricately embedded with shimmering shell motifs of florals, birds, and mythical creatures, such pieces blended Chinese artistry with local influences, serving both decorative and practical purposes within the household.

Mother-of-pearl, cut from the iridescent inner lining of marine mollusc shells and set against the deep grain of ebony, is the material that gives this furniture its character. Guangdong was a major centre of mother-of-pearl inlay, producing luxury furniture for Chinese communities whose commercial networks extended across maritime Southeast Asia. At the same time, the craft was also practised locally by Chinese artisans who temporarily resided or settled in the region. The technique shared a common foundation with traditions such as Thai khruang pradab muk -- shells gathered from coastal waters were cut, shaped, and set against a dark surface to create intricate, contrasting patterns.

The Peranakan Chinese, a culturally hybrid community shaped by interactions between Chinese and Malay worlds, developed domestic styles that reflected their cosmopolitan identities. Wealthy households combined Chinese decorative motifs with Western furniture forms, creating interiors that expressed both ancestral connections and participation in global trade networks. Here, for instance, the vertical Chinese scroll format is framed in the Western fashion. At the same time, exported Cantonese furniture from the late Qing and early Republican periods also reflected its own processes of adaptation, incorporating Western Rococo forms and marquetry techniques while retaining traditional Chinese woodworking practices.

In Peranakan households across Malacca, Singapore, Penang, and the wider region, furniture like this marked wealth accumulated through trade. The mother-of-pearl embedded in its surface — the shell of a marine creature, worked by craftsmen in southern China — travelled to Southeast Asia as part of the same maritime networks through which the Peranakan communities themselves had moved, settled, and built the material world of their homes.

In Peranakan homes across Malacca, Singapore, Penang, and the wider region, furniture such as this became a visible expression of wealth, taste, and social position. The mother-of-pearl that illuminates its surface, in particular, embodies the same process that defined Peranakan material culture: the adaptation of elements from across the maritime world into a distinct regional identity.

objects.title: Neptune Cup Sponge
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum
objects.caption:
The Neptune Cup Sponge (Cliona patera) is shaped like a cup or goblet, growing to over a metre in both height and diameter — a scale, by some accounts, large enough for a small child to sit inside its basin. It lives in marine soft sediment habitats across the Indo-West Pacific, with populations recorded in Singapore, Thailand, and the islands of Koh Rong Sanloem and Koh Koun in Cambodia. The Neptune Sponge was described by the naturalist Thomas Hardwicke in 1820, thus making it the first sponge species formally described from the island of Singapore. Its unusual shape and immense size captured scientific and public attention for the next two centuries.

This specimen in the LKCNHM was collected more than 100 years ago, from a time when the sponge was still a familiar presence in regional waters. Its elegant goblet-like form and unusual size made it a coveted museum specimen, fuelling over-collection and rapid decline: abundant in the early 1900s, it had gone entirely unseen by the late 1900s.

In 2011, two living Neptune Cup Sponges were discovered in the Singapore Straits, within a marine environment heavily transformed by coastal reclamation. Since then, populations have been found in various parts of Southeast Asia. In a region where coastal environments are under sustained pressure, the Neptune Cup Sponge's reappearance in profoundly altered waters is a reminder that the natural world can still surprise.

objects.title: Phra Upagutta Enshrined in a Conch Shell
objects.title_raw: Phra Upagutta Enshrined in a Conch Shell
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
Cast entirely from brass, this small amulet depicts the Arhat Upagutta seated in meditation, his hands pressed together in prayer (Phanam Mue), enclosed within a hollowed conch shell. Its surface has developed a coppery-bronze patina over time. The conch bears the rare clockwise Dakkhinavarta (Thaksinawat) spiral, a form regarded in Buddhist and Hindu traditions as an auspicious emblem of cosmic order and balance.

Within Southern Thai folk Buddhism, Upagutta is venerated as the supreme guardian of monastic rituals, a subduer of Mara, and a protector against forces beyond human control. According to Buddhist legend, he resides in a state of deep meditative absorption (Nirodha-samapatti) at the “Navel of the Sea” (Sado Thale), beneath the mythical ocean. Enclosing his image within a sea conch — a vessel already associated with sacred power, water, and divine presence — transforms the amulet into a kind of portable temple. It brings together the protective power of Upagutta and the spiritual potency attributed to the ocean itself.

The veneration of Upagutta originated in India and travelled through Mon, Burmese, and Lanna regions before reaching Southern Thailand and the Malay Peninsula. In coastal communities, where livelihoods depended on fishing, maritime trade, and journeys across uncertain waters, his role developed particular significance. Once associated with the protection of large public ceremonies and invoked through state ritual, Upagutta’s image was transformed into a personal amulet carried by merchants, sailors, and others seeking safety and prosperity.

The transformation of a sea shell into a dwelling place for a Buddhist guardian reflects a broader Southeast Asian pattern in which protective beliefs from different traditions became layered within a single object. The conch’s associations with the power of the sea and the natural world were combined with Buddhist ideas of spiritual guardianship. Together they created an amulet carried by coastal communities as they crossed uncertain waters -- literal or metaphorical.

objects.title: Sacred Conch Shell
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This sacred conch shell (Turbinella pyrum),  known in Thai as hoi sang and in Sanskrit as shankha, features an elegant teardrop silhouette, a thick, highly calcified exterior, and a smooth, hollow interior whorl. This geometry — naturally suited to hold water, to sound as a horn, and to spiral in directions that carry cosmological meaning — has made the conch a vessel of religious significance in South and Southeast Asia for millennia.

In the daily folk traditions of Southern Thailand, the conch is closely associated with rituals centred on sacred hydrology, where water is regarded as an element of cosmic purity and the source of biological life. To enhance this auspicious quality, many Southern Thai households introduce sacred sweet-scented bael leaves (Bai Matoom) into the conch’s reservoir during domestic lustration ceremonies. Beyond household rituals, the conch also serves as a symbol of good fortune and material prosperity among coastal merchants, shopkeepers, and fishermen. As an object originating from the sea, a realm associated with abundance and wealth, it is believed to attract commercial success and ensure the continued flow of fortune. Merchants commonly place sacred conches on storefront altars or sales counters to bless daily transactions. Sometimes they place coins, gold leaf, or miniature talismans inside the shell’s aperture to enhance its auspicious power.

In Brahmanical-Hindu cosmology, the conch shell is a foundational symbol for Vishnu, the protector of the universe. He holds the conch shell in one of his four hands, along with the discus, the mace, and the lotus. The conch represents the primordial sound of creation. Vedic mythology records that Vishnu descended into the abyssal depths to retrieve sacred texts from a demon concealed inside a conch, thereby infusing the shell with absolute spiritual purity. As such, any water passing through its chamber is transformed into a holy purificatory medium. This cosmology entered Southeast Asia through centuries of trade and migration. It merged with indigenous beliefs to make the conch the primary vessel for consecrated water (Nam Mon) across major life-transition ceremonies, including monastic lustration, housewarmings, and wedding rituals. The practice of Sang Rot Nam, pouring sacred water from the mouth of a conch onto the hands of a bride and groom, remains a foundational matrimonial rite in contemporary Thailand.

Among conches, the highest status belongs to the rare clockwise, right-spiralling shell. Revered as an exceptional natural form associated with cosmic blessing, right-whorled specimens were traditionally reserved for important state and religious ceremonies, including the royal coronations. Along the Maritime Silk Road, conch shells circulated as premium luxury commodities and high-status diplomatic tribute presented to regional kings. As they entered coastal settlements across the Thai-Malay Peninsula, they were continually reinterpreted, dissolving the boundaries between natural object, religious doctrine, and maritime life.

This natural conch shell thus stands as a vital material archive documenting the synthesis of deep Vedic cosmology, maritime commerce, and local folk traditions across South and Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Shell Beads / Blood Cockle (Anadara granosa)
objects.caption:
These shell beads, fashioned from blood cockle (Anadara granosa) shells, and dating to the prehistoric period, were discovered at the Khok Phanom Di archaeological site in Chonburi Province, Thailand. The blood cockle is found throughout the Indo-Pacific region, from the eastern coast of South Africa northward and eastward through Southeast Asia, Australia, Polynesia, and up to northern Japan.

Shells have held significance in Southeast Asia from prehistoric times. Before the arrival of organized religions, shells served as food, resources, and tools for coastal and riverine communities, and certain types were used to make ornaments, containers, and implements. Because of this, shells became symbols of life, fertility, and the abundance of nature.

The use of shells as ornaments reflects an understanding of them as something more than raw material: objects worn on the body, associated with the sea, and placed in contexts that point toward a significance beyond the everyday. In addition, the presence of shell ornaments in areas beyond the coast indicates trade contact between coastal and inland communities. It also suggests that these small marine objects already functioned as markers of exchange and connection across distances.

Today the blood cockle remains economically important in Thailand. Its meat is widely consumed as a rich source of protein, commonly prepared by grilling or blanching, while its shells are used for ornaments and souvenirs and processed for lime production. In the blood cockle beads from Khok Phanom Di, however, a much older relationship is preserved — the sea's materials entering the social life of the region, carried on the body, at the beginning of a long history of shared meaning.

objects.title: Unglazed Stoneware Conches
objects.caption:
These unglazed stoneware vessels, shaped in the form of a conch shell, were a ritual utensil used in Vajrayana (Tantric) Buddhist practice. Water held within the vessel was regarded as sacred, used in rites of purification, blessing, and consecration.

The choice of the conch form was significant. Across South and Southeast Asia, the shell was associated with water, fertility, and life. In Hinduism, the conch is one of the symbols of Vishnu, blown to begin ceremonies or proclaim victories. In Buddhism, it is one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols, representing the sound of the Buddha’s teachings or Dharma.

Buriram Province, where this vessel was produced, formed part of the Khmer Empire, whose courts and religious centres fostered a rich tradition of Hindu-Buddhist ritual practice. In Khmer culture, the conch shell (shankha) was associated with sacred sound, divine authority, and ceremonial proclamation. Khmer artisans transformed the natural shell into fired clay vessels that could both hold consecrated water and serve as ritual instruments.  Their sound was believed to connect the human world with the divine realm. At sacred sites such as Angkor Wat, water poured from conch vessels was used in ceremonies of purification and consecration, while conches were blown during the worship of deities and the commencement of ceremonies. These associations also made the conch an important element of royal ritual, where it expressed the sacred authority and legitimacy of the king.

This stoneware conch from Buriram thus reflects how Khmer artisans adapted a natural marine form into a ritual object suited to the shared religious and political worlds of their time. Its use builds upon longstanding associations of the conch across Southeast Asia. Shells from the sea had long carried meanings of fertility and life, and later became vessels through which Hindu-Buddhist traditions expressed purification and divine authority.

objects.title: Buffalo-shaped Water Container
objects.caption:
This hand-built, ox-shaped pottery vessel still bears the fingerprints of its maker, with clearly incised features of a water buffalo and an opening on the back to serve as a container. Made of low-fired earthenware using coils of clay to construct the walls, it was most likely used during important ceremonies or for burial purposes. The vessel is sturdy, with distinctly formed eyes, nose, mouth, ears, and nearly symmetrical horns.
Objects and motifs depicting the water buffalo were common among prehistoric communities in Southeast Asia, particularly those associated with wet-rice cultivation. In these farming communities, the buffalo was likely an essential beast of burden, serving as a symbol of a farmer's wealth as well as animistic worship.

objects.title: Calapa with Buffalo Shape
objects.caption:
This calapa, made of copper and shaped in the form of a buffalo, was traditionally used by Bruneians to store betel nuts, and over time also to keep jewellery. Today it is mainly displayed as a decorative item and preserved in museums as part of Brunei's cultural heritage.

The buffalo (Bubalus bubalis) was one of the most important animals in the agricultural landscape of inland Brunei, particularly among paddy-farming communities. Farmers relied on buffaloes to clear fields for cultivation, and transport heavy loads, including small boats known as kuntul. As the animal that enabled wet-rice agriculture, the buffalo came to represent strength, endurance, and the productive abundance generated through human and animal cooperation.

Shaping a vessel for betel nut in the form of a buffalo brought these associations into the realm of hospitality and social prestige. Across the Malay world, betel was offered during important encounters as a gesture of respect, welcome, and relationship-building, and the containers used to hold its ingredients could themselves become objects of display. By transforming the agricultural animal that sustained the community into a finely crafted copper possession, this calapa linked material prosperity with the forces that produced it: the strength of the buffalo, the fertility of the land, and the abundance that supported social life.

The buffalo form therefore turned this familiar working animal into a symbol of prosperity and continuity, showing how Southeast Asian communities elevated the creatures that sustained their livelihoods into objects of cultural value and prestige.

objects.title: Perminaken
objects.caption:
Known among the Batak peoples of northern Sumatra as a buli-buli, this medicine horn, or perminaken (from minak, meaning "medicine"), is carved from the hollow horn of a Sumatran serow. It was used by a datu (ritual specialist) to store ritually potent substances prepared from roots, leaves, bark, animal materials, and other ingredients. 
These medicines were believed to protect, heal, or, when required, harm. Carried from the shoulder or belt, the horn kept these substances close at hand during ritual practice.

The seated figure carved on the stopper may represent a predecessor in a lineage of ritual specialists or a mythical figure found on other Batak ritual objects. Similar carvings also appear on megalithic sculptures from northern Sumatra, linking this vessel to wider artistic and ceremonial traditions.

Across the Batak communities of northern Sumatra, spiritual authority rested with the datu, whose specialised knowledge of ritual and medicine complemented the civic authority of local leaders. The buli-buli was therefore both a practical container and an emblem of ritual expertise.

objects.title: Sumatran Serow
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum
objects.caption: The Sumatran serow (Capricornis sumatraensis) is a rugged goat-antelope that lives on steep, forested mountains in Sumatra and the Thai-Malay Peninsula. It can be identified by its coarse dark coat, pale patches on the throat and face, a stiff upright mane, and short, slightly curved horns that both males and females have. This skull specimen is on display at the LKCNHM gallery. Serows are found in rugged rainforest between about 200 and 3,000 meters in elevation. They are able to move confidently along cliffs and rocky ledges, often staying near hillsides and caves which give them shelter and safe vantage points. Because they need large, connected areas of wild hillside forest, their presence helps scientists judge how healthy and intact these landscapes are. The serow is well-known across Sumatra. In local languages it is sometimes called the "forest goat," and it appears in stories about their amazing climbing skills. Tales have been told of how serows sleep while hanging by their horns or hook their horns into rock to scale cliffs, highlighting their agility, even if they are not literally true. Historically, serows have been hunted for food and for parts used in traditional medicine. Illegal trade continues to threaten them in Indonesia despite existing laws. The Sumatran serow is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, mainly due to poaching and habitat loss. Protecting steep forest habitats, limiting road-building, and stopping illegal trade are key steps to keep this unique mountain mammal from disappearing.

objects.title: Blue-and-White Qinghua Porcelain Plate
objects.caption:
Decorated with two phoenixes surrounded by scrolling foliage, this blue-and-white porcelain plate is an example of the high-quality Chinese ceramics that travelled throughout maritime Southeast Asia. Produced during the Ming dynasty using cobalt underglaze painting and high-temperature firing techniques, it was recovered from the Brunei Shipwreck Site, a reminder of the extensive maritime networks linking China with Southeast Asian ports.

During the early sultanate period, Brunei was an important centre of regional trade, connecting merchants, goods, and artistic traditions across the South China Sea. Chinese ceramics such as this plate were prestige objects, valued by royal courts, elites, and wealthy households for feasting, display, and ceremonial occasions.

The phoenix motif carried powerful associations in Chinese culture. As a symbol of virtue, harmony, and imperial refinement, it was traditionally linked to feminine authority and the empress.  In Brunei, however, the phoenix could also be appreciated beyond its original imperial meaning — as a refined and auspicious decorative motif. This plate demonstrates how objects moving through maritime trade networks carried symbols that were continuously interpreted and adapted by communities across Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Covered Box Decorated with Phoenixes
objects.caption:
This covered stoneware box is the only known, complete Vietnamese vessel decorated with phoenixes. Produced in northern Vietnam during the 15th century, its dark blue glaze and design’s precise alignment across box and cover indicate that it was likely a specially commissioned object, possibly intended as a diplomatic gift.

The phoenix held a particularly elevated position in Vietnamese and Chinese courtly traditions. Associated with the empress, feminine authority, virtue, and refinement, it was a symbol reserved for contexts connected with status and ceremony. Its presence on a carefully crafted covered vessel transformed the object from a functional container into an expression of prestige and cultivated identity.

The phoenix motif also reflects the movement of shared visual traditions across East and Southeast Asia. While rooted in Chinese cosmology, the symbol was adopted and reinterpreted by Vietnamese courts, where it was considered as one of the Four Mythical Creatures (Tứ Linh), and became part of local expressions of power, diplomacy, and refinement.

The phoenix transformed this functional vessel into a statement of prestige, signalling the refinement and status of its owner. Its presence in prestige goods produced in Vietnam shows how symbols originating in Chinese imperial culture were selectively adopted and reinterpreted within Southeast Asian material culture.

objects.title: Kam Cheng
objects.caption:
This ornate porcelain kam cheng is a covered storage jar traditionally used among Peranakan Chinese communities. Such vessels were valued not only for storing food but also for their decorative presence within the household, where objects used in daily life often carried wishes for prosperity, harmony, and family well-being.
The jar is decorated with phoenixes and peonies — a pairing rich in Chinese symbolic meaning. The phoenix represents grace, virtue, harmony, and feminine refinement, while the peony symbolises honour, wealth, and flourishing. Together, they express aspirations for a prosperous and harmonious household.

The yellow enamel background further enhances the jar’s auspicious character. Traditionally associated with imperial authority, yellow also became widely used in celebratory contexts among Peranakan communities, particularly during occasions such as weddings, birthdays, and festivals. These jars were often used to serve ceremonial foods, including nasi kemuli (spiced rice), linking the symbolism of the phoenix directly with acts of hospitality and family celebration.

Through the incorporation of the phoenix on its surface, this vessel reveals how symbols once associated with imperial authority were transformed into part of everyday domestic life. In Peranakan households across maritime Southeast Asia, the bird became a familiar expression of prosperity, harmony, and cultural identity.

objects.title: Offering Dish
objects.caption:
This porcelain offering dish was made for ritual use, not ordinary dining. Its thickly potted body, twelve-lobed fluted rim, and richly decorated surface reflect the importance placed on vessels used in acts of devotion. The dish is painted with phoenixes among peonies, while the inner rim features the Eight Auspicious Buddhist Emblems — symbols associated with blessings, protection, and spiritual well-being.

In Chinese tradition, the phoenix (fenghuang) is an auspicious creature associated with grace, virtue, harmony, and high status. Unlike a bird of the natural world, it is a composite being described through features of different animals -- the neck of a snake, a swallow's breast, a tortoise's back, and a fish's tail -- embodying the perfection of many qualities. Its five-coloured plumage and harmonious song reflect cosmic balance, while its association with the empress positioned it as a symbol of feminine virtue and authority.

On ritual vessels such as this, the phoenix carried wishes for harmony between the human and spiritual worlds. The accompanying peony,  a flower associated with honour, prosperity, and beauty, reinforces these auspicious meanings. During the late Qing period, altar vessels decorated with such imagery were used in ancestral and religious ceremonies, where offerings of food were presented as acts of remembrance and devotion.

Through the phoenix, a creature of imperial and cosmological significance entered the intimate space of ritual practice, allowing communities in Southeast Asia to express hopes for harmony, continuity, and divine blessing through the objects used to honour their ancestors and the sacred.

objects.title: Pending (รอไฟล์)
objects.collection: The Perak Museum, Department of Museums Malaysia
objects.caption:
This pending is a distinctive belt buckle worn by Malay and Baba Nyonya (Peranakan) communities While forms and materials vary, the pending has long served as more than a functional fastening for the samping (sarong): its design, ornamentation, and symbolism communicated the wearer’s social standing, wealth, and identity.

Among Malay communities, the characteristic ogival (eye-shaped) form of the pending was associated with power and prestige. Historically, the pending also carried practical and protective functions: it secured a man's samping, shielded the body from the keris in times of conflict, and, when inscribed with Quranic verses or combined with amulets, was believed to guard the wearer from harm.

Among Baba Nyonya communities, pendings developed into highly decorative heirloom objects, often incorporating intricate motifs drawn from both Malay and Chinese visual traditions. Bird imagery featured prominently in Peranakan ornament, where birds symbolised prosperity, beauty, harmony, and auspicious fortune. Rendered on a prestige object worn close to the body, these birds transformed natural forms into signs of refinement and social aspiration.

The bird motifs on Baba Nyonya pendings also reveal the layered cultural exchanges that shaped the Malay Archipelago. Combining Malay traditions of personal adornment with Chinese-inspired decorative symbolism, these objects demonstrate how communities across maritime Southeast Asia adapted shared visual languages to express their own identities. As a wearable marker of status, the pending shows how animals could move from the natural world into the realm of prestige — carrying meanings of prosperity, protection, and belonging across generations.

objects.title: Porcelain Plate Depicting Phoenix
objects.caption:
This plate is an example of Peranakan Chinese porcelain, or Nyonya ware, made from overglaze polychrome porcelain. It carries the reign mark "Xuantong nian zhi," referring to the Xuantong Emperor Puyi, who reigned from 1908 to 1911, suggesting the piece was produced during that period. The bright yellow background is an auspicious colour among Peranakan Chinese, associated with festive occasions such as Chinese New Year and birthday celebrations.

The central decorative motif is a phoenix perched on a moss-covered rockery from which blossoming peonies grow. The phoenix is brightly coloured, its neck plumage and feathers painted in blue, red and green strokes. In Chinese culture, the phoenix represents beauty, grace and high virtue, and symbolises the bride or the empress. When depicted perched on a rockery, it also connotes stability and permanence. The peony alongside it is a symbol of spring, love, beauty and good fortune. At the edges of the dish are symbols drawn from the Eight Auspicious Symbols of Buddhism, including the unending knot, the lotus flower, the pair of golden fish and the conch shell.

Produced in British Malaya for Peranakan Chinese households, this plate reflects the movement of Chinese artistic traditions through maritime Southeast Asia. The phoenix, originally embedded within imperial Chinese visual language, was transformed into a familiar symbol within domestic life far beyond the court. On this plate, it appears alongside Buddhist imagery and festive decorative traditions, reflecting the layered identities of Peranakan communities shaped by Chinese heritage, local Southeast Asian environments, and centuries of cultural exchange.

The presence of the phoenix on a household object from colonial Malaya demonstrates how animals and symbols travelled alongside people, goods, and ideas across the region. No longer confined to imperial or elite settings, the phoenix became part of everyday expressions of family prosperity, social identity, and cultural continuity among Chinese communities throughout maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Tiga Negeri Cloth
objects.caption:
Tiga Negeri batik is a celebrated textile tradition that developed along the north coast of Java. Its name, meaning "three regions," refers to a distinctive dyeing process that combined the finest natural pigments from three renowned batik centres: the deep red (merah getih pithik) of Lasem, the indigo blue of Pekalongan, and the soga brown of Solo. The resulting cloth brought together the colours, techniques, and artistic traditions of these centres in a single textile, creating hybrid designs that blend inland (pedalaman) and coastal (pesisiran) batik aesthetics.

Classified as a form of Peranakan batik, Tiga Negeri textiles often feature the phoenix (burung hong), alongside floral and botanical motifs and the intricate isen-isen (decorative filler patterns) characteristic of inland Javanese batik. The phoenix entered Java through long histories of interaction between Chinese and Southeast Asian communities. In Chinese tradition, it symbolises virtue, beauty, harmony, and feminine grace, while within Peranakan communities it also came to represent domestic prosperity and refinement, appearing on textiles, ceramics, and household objects.

On this cloth, the phoenix reflects the movement of ideas alongside materials. Reinterpreted through Javanese craftsmanship and Peranakan artistic traditions, it became part of the multicultural visual language of coastal Java, demonstrating how communities continually adapted shared motifs through local creativity and exchange.

objects.title: Batik Hokokai Long Cloth
objects.caption:
Hokokai batik emerged in Java during the Japanese occupation of Indonesia (1942–1945), reflecting the encounter between Javanese batik traditions and Japanese aesthetics. Its name derives from Jawa Hokokai, an organisation established by the Japanese administration during the occupation.

Hokokai textiles are distinguished by their finely detailed designs and elaborate motifs, including flowers, butterflies, and peacocks. The peacock is commonly associated with beauty and elegance, while the butterfly reflects motifs that had long circulated through Chinese artistic traditions, where it symbolises love and harmony.

The cloth also features the distinctive pagi sore ("morning–evening") design, which combines two contrasting compositions on a single textile. Developed during a period of material shortages, this ingenious format allowed the cloth to be worn in different ways, creating the impression of multiple garments. The susomoyo border motif, adapted from the decorative hems of Japanese furisode and tomesode kimono, further illustrates how Javanese artisans incorporated and reinterpreted new artistic influences within the batik tradition

objects.title: Betel Box Set of Sultan Abdul Samad
objects.title_raw: Betel Box Set of Sultan Abdul Samad
objects.caption:
This betel set is believed to have belonged to Sultan Abdul Samad Ibni Almarhum Raja Abdullah (1859–1880), the fourth Sultan of Selangor. It is thought to have been used during palace ceremonies, including the reception of distinguished guests, royal weddings, and coronations, occasions where the offering of betel expressed respect, hospitality, and social relationships.

The most distinctive element is the betel nut slicer (kacip sireh), whose blade is fashioned in the form of a horse's head. The rest of the set is equally elaborate, with moth carvings at the corners of the lid, a floral bouquet in the central medallion, and scalloped floral motifs around the edges. Through its craftsmanship and imagery, the set transforms an everyday object associated with betel preparation into one used for ceremonial display.

Across maritime Southeast Asia, the offering and receiving of betel was an important social practice. The choice of vessel, the manner of presentation, and the relationship between host and guest all communicated status, respect, and political relationships. In ceremonial settings such as this one, a finely crafted betel set expressed both the refinement of its makers and the standing of those who exchanged it.

Within Malay court traditions, the horse was associated with nobility, military ability, and social status. Introduced through networks linking the Malay world with India, China, and mainland Southeast Asia, horses became valued prestige animals. In Java, they are recorded as symbols of status from as early as the seventh century, and by the nineteenth century they remained important markers of elite identity as well as valued diplomatic gifts.

The bird shaped kacip sireh brought these associations into the shared ritual of offering betel. By combining the symbolism of the bird with the craftsmanship of the betel set, it transformed a functional implement into an expression of abundance and prestige. The bird shape also reflects the movement of ideas, animals, and artistic traditions across the communities of maritime Southeast Asia.

objects.title: Garment for Buddhist Prostration, Featuring Garuda and Peacock Motifs (Na Muen Si Supplementary Weft Textile)
objects.title_raw: Garment for Buddhist Prostration, Featuring Garuda and  Peacock Motifs (Na Muen Si Supplementary Weft Textile)
title_variants: Garment for Buddhist Prostration, Featuring Garuda and Peacock Motifs (Na Muen Si Supplementary Weft Textile)
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This ceremonial textile from Na Muen Si, Trang Province, is a Buddhist prostration cloth (Luk Pha) woven with Garuda and peacock motifs using the intricate supplementary weft (Yok Dok) technique. Created by master weaver Mrs. Plek Nuiphol, the cloth features raised golden-yellow patterns against a deep red ground, a colour combination traditionally reserved for important ritual textiles in Southern Thailand. During Buddhist ceremonies, the textile was placed on the floor where devotees knelt to prostrate before Buddha images or senior monks. This act transformed an ordinary physical space into a sacred one, expressing reverence towards the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha.

The textile’s significance lies not only in its craftsmanship but also in the animals woven into its surface. The Garuda (Khrut), the mythical king of birds, has long represented divine protection, strength, and the defence of Buddhist teachings across Hindu-Buddhist traditions in Southeast Asia. The peacock (Nok Yung), meanwhile, symbolises beauty, purity, and spiritual discipline. In Buddhist stories, the peacock is associated with overcoming desire and cultivating wisdom. Its ability to remain radiant despite consuming poisonous plants became a metaphor for transforming worldly difficulties into spiritual strength.

Placed together, the Garuda and peacock create a powerful ritual pairing. The Garuda offers protection and celestial power, while the peacock embodies inner purity and moral cultivation. Their presence on a prostration cloth reflects the devotee’s own spiritual journey: approaching the sacred space under protection while seeking purification and enlightenment.

The Na Muen Si weaving tradition preserves the memory of how these motifs entered local textile culture. According to community oral history, the master weaver Yai Fai Sukhong was inspired by the Garuda emblems displayed on official buildings and the auspicious birds depicted in temples in Trang’s provincial centre. She adapted these images into complex woven patterns, translating symbols of royal and religious authority into textiles created within village communities. Through generations of weaving, these motifs became part of the visual language of Southern Thai Buddhist life.

Beyond its use as a prostration cloth, textiles featuring Garuda and peacock motifs could also accompany major life rituals. Some were used as ceremonial cloths covering coffins, where the sacred birds were understood as celestial beings capable of guiding the deceased towards the afterlife. In this context, the Garuda and peacock served as spiritual companions whose qualities helped connect human life with the divine realm.

The presence of these birds in Na Muen Si textiles also reflects a wider Southeast Asian heritage. Across the region, from royal emblems and temple architecture to ritual objects and textiles, the Garuda and peacock have served as shared symbols of protection and virtue. Woven into this single piece of cloth, they reveal how communities across Southeast Asia adapted common religious and artistic traditions into local expressions of faith, identity, and devotion.

objects.title: Green Peafowl
objects.collection: Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum
objects.caption:
The green peafowl (Pavo muticus) is a large pheasant native to mainland Southeast Asia, including Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam and parts of Indonesia, particularly Java. Distinguished by its iridescent green plumage, long train and striking crest, it is one of the most spectacular bird species in the region. Unlike the more familiar Indian peafowl, both male and female green peafowl possess green neck plumage, although the males are larger and have longer ornamental trains used in courtship displays.

Green peafowl inhabit a variety of environments, including open forests, grasslands, riverine habitats and forest edges. They forage on the ground for seeds, fruits, shoots, insects, reptiles and other small animals. During the breeding season, males perform elaborate displays, fanning their trains and producing loud calls to attract females and defend their territories.

Throughout Southeast Asia, the green peafowl has long been associated with royalty, beauty and spiritual significance. In Javanese tradition, peafowl feathers were symbols of nobility and prestige, while in parts of mainland Southeast Asia the bird appears in folklore, temple art and ceremonial decorations. Its elegant appearance has made it a recurring motif in traditional textiles, carvings and architecture.

Historically widespread across Southeast Asia, the green peafowl has experienced significant population declines due to hunting, habitat loss and agricultural expansion. Today, it is classified as Endangered (EN) on the IUCN Red List, surviving mainly in fragmented populations within protected areas. Conservation efforts across the region aim to safeguard the species and its remaining habitats. The species reflects the rich avian heritage of Southeast Asia and serves as a reminder of the importance of conserving the region's remaining forest ecosystems.

objects.title: Kalakati
objects.caption:
This copper betel cutter from Brunei Darussalam features a handle shaped as a bird’s head, with the body decorated with geometric and floral motifs. Traditionally used to cut betel nut (pinang) and local fruits, such cutters were once part of the material culture of hospitality and daily social exchange. Today, this example is valued primarily as a decorative object, preserving the craftsmanship and symbolism embedded in its form.

In Bruneian Malay society, birds were closely observed as part of the natural rhythms that governed agricultural life. The seasonal presence and behaviour of birds around paddy fields and waterways helped communities interpret environmental changes, including when to begin or delay farming activities. Species such as egrets, herons, mynas, fantails, swallows, and tailorbirds were familiar companions within these landscapes, their movements forming part of local ecological knowledge.

The bird’s head carved onto the handle of this betel cutter therefore carries meanings beyond decoration. As a crafted element on an object associated with hospitality, refinement, and social interaction, it elevates a functional tool into a marker of cultural knowledge and aesthetic value. The bird connects the prestige of the object to the natural world from which communities drew their understanding of time, season, and place.

Although the exact species represented cannot be identified, the bird would have been immediately recognisable to its users as a familiar presence from Brunei’s fields and waterways. Here, the bird that guided agricultural rhythms became the bird that adorned a valued possession, showing how animals in Southeast Asian societies could move between the practical knowledge of everyday life and the symbolic language of prestige and identity.

objects.title: Noken
objects.caption:
This noken, a traditional net bag from Papua, is woven from natural fibres and adorned with cassowary feet and strands of wild boar tail hair. Across Papuan communities, noken are widely used to carry everyday goods and are traditionally worn by suspending the bag from the head. The addition of cassowary feet distinguishes this example from everyday noken, marking it as an object associated with leadership and social status.

The cassowary is a powerful flightless bird native to New Guinea, the Moluccas, and northeastern Australia. Known for its strong legs, sharp claws, and ability to move rapidly through dense rainforest, it has long been understood by Papuan communities as a creature of exceptional strength and spiritual potency. Although often described as the world's most dangerous bird, the cassowary is a shy species that inhabits humid tropical forests. Its body parts carry meanings beyond their physical form, embodying the qualities associated with the animal itself.

By incorporating cassowary feet into a noken, these qualities become part of the object's social meaning. Worn close to the body and carried in a prominent position, the bag expresses the strength, protection, vitality, and ancestral connections associated with the cassowary. In this way, the animal's qualities become visible through an object that signifies leadership and social standing.

This relationship between people, animals, and material culture can be found in many parts of Southeast Asia. Communities across the region incorporated feathers, claws, horns, teeth, and other animal materials into objects associated with leadership, status, ancestry, and spiritual power. In this noken, the cassowary's feet transform the strength of one of Papua's most distinctive birds into a visible expression of social hierarchy.

objects.title: Pending (Traditional Belt Buckle)
objects.collection: The National Textile Museum, Department of Museums Malaysia
objects.caption:
This pending is a distinctive belt buckle worn by Malay and Baba Nyonya (Peranakan) communities While forms and materials vary, the pending has long served as more than a functional fastening for the samping (sarong): its design, ornamentation, and symbolism communicated the wearer’s social standing, wealth, and identity.

Among Malay communities, the characteristic ogival (eye-shaped) form of the pending was associated with power and prestige. Historically, the pending also carried practical and protective functions: it secured a man's samping, shielded the body from the keris in times of conflict, and, when inscribed with Quranic verses or combined with amulets, was believed to guard the wearer from harm.

Among Baba Nyonya communities, pendings developed into highly decorative heirloom objects, often incorporating intricate motifs drawn from both Malay and Chinese visual traditions. Bird imagery featured prominently in Peranakan ornament, where birds symbolised prosperity, beauty, harmony, and auspicious fortune. Rendered on a prestige object worn close to the body, these birds transformed natural forms into signs of refinement and social aspiration.

The bird motifs on Baba Nyonya pendings also reveal the layered cultural exchanges that shaped the Malay Archipelago. Combining Malay traditions of personal adornment with Chinese-inspired decorative symbolism, these objects demonstrate how communities across maritime Southeast Asia adapted shared visual languages to express their own identities. As a wearable marker of status, the pending shows how animals could move from the natural world into the realm of prestige — carrying meanings of prosperity, protection, and belonging across generations.

objects.title: Quail-Shaped Silver Casket
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.caption:
This small silver casket, produced by silversmiths in Thailand’s Nakhon Si Thammarat Province, is shaped to mimic the organic profile of a quail, with a plump, rounded body and an upturned head. The structure is horizontally bisected into an upper lid and a lower base that fits flush together, sealing the small items kept inside. It was produced using metal casting combined with detailed repoussé and chasing techniques (Salak Dun) on sheet silver. The smith hammered the sheet from the reverse to create three-dimensional depth, then chased fine details onto the outer surface to delineate the wings, anatomical posture and delicate plumage of the bird.

The quail (Nok Khum) is elevated in Southern Thai folklore beyond its status as a common bird to become an auspicious symbol of protection, particularly against fires. This belief links directly to the Vattaka Jataka, a tale from the canonical Buddhist Jataka literature well known to the local population. The text recounts a past life of the Buddha, reborn as a young quail nesting in a wild forest. One day, a fierce wildfire swept toward the nest. While his parents flew away to save themselves, the fledgling, still unable to fly, faced the flames alone. Making an Act of Truth (Sacca-adhitthana) grounded in the purity of his virtues, he commanded the fire to retreat, and the forest fire instantly extinguished. The quail thereafter became a celebrated regional symbol of safe-keeping, misfortune evasion, loving-kindness, and protective grace.

Functionally, this casket held the ingredients of betel-quid chewing — areca nuts, betel leaves, slaked lime paste and shredded tobacco — a practice that in traditional Thai and Malay societies was bound up with formal social etiquette, guest reception and diplomatic hospitality. Receptacles designed to hold these ingredients were crafted with the same artistic care as fine jewellery or weapon scabbards. And that this casket takes the form of the fire-extinguishing quail of the Jatakas is not incidental: the protective bird was brought into the domestic space as a functional spiritual choice, not just a decorative one.

In Southern Thai manuscript culture, accordion-folded bark books (Nang Prueat or Nang Sue Bot) frequently recorded the Quail Yantra (Yant Nok Khum). These esoteric diagrams feature geometric interpretations of the quail surrounded by sacred Khmer script and protective incantations (Katha). They were installed to shield households from fire and disaster. The story that circulated through the Theravada Buddhist world as a Jataka narrative was thus adapted in Southern Thailand into esoteric manuscript diagrams and then into three-dimensional silverware. These adaptations show how a single canonical Buddhist text, shared across communities from South to Southeast Asia, generated distinct but connected forms of protective material culture.

objects.title: Garuda Sculptures
objects.caption:
The Garuda, the great bird-like being and mount of the Hindu god Vishnu, is one of Southeast Asia’s most enduring mythological figures. Across Hindu traditions, Garuda embodies strength, knowledge, courage, loyalty, and discipline, while his role as Vishnu’s vehicle connects him with the preservation of cosmic order.

One of the most famous episodes involving Garuda appears in the Indian epic Ramayana. During Rama’s battle against the demon king Ravana, the latter’s son Indrajit uses the magical serpent weapon known as the nagapasha to bind Rama and his brother Lakshmana, leaving them powerless. Suddenly, a great storm descends upon the battlefield, and from the sky emerges Garuda, whose very presence terrifies the serpents that form the weapon’s bindings. As Garuda approaches, the serpent arrows release their hold, and he restores Rama and Lakshmana’s strength by touching their wounds.

Although this story belongs to a world of divine beings and mythical creatures, it also reflects close observations of the natural world. The ancient association between Garuda and serpents echoes the real relationship between large birds of prey and snakes, where birds were understood as protectors against creatures associated with danger. As Hindu epics travelled to Southeast Asia, where such natural dynamics apply too, this episode was preserved, including in versions of the Ramayana such as the Thai Ramakien, where Garuda continued to represent protection, power, and victory over harmful forces.

This wooden sculpture from the Ada Guna Museum depicts the Hindu god Vishnu seated upon his mount Garuda. Shown as a hybrid being with the body of a human and the features of a bird, Garuda carries Vishnu — the preserver of the universe — while both figures are adorned with crowns and jewellery that signify divine and royal authority. In Bali and the wider Java region, rulers were often associated with Vishnu and his incarnations, linking kingship with the deity’s role in maintaining harmony and order.

This is a contemporary interpretation of similar garuda figures that were incorporated into Balinese sacred spaces, architectural elements, ritual objects, or standalone sculptures. Their presence reflected the Hindu-Buddhist cosmology in which temples represented a connection between the earthly and divine realms, while sacred beings such as Garuda served as protectors of that boundary. The sculpture therefore represents not only a religious image, but also the long process through which Southeast Asian communities transformed shared mythological traditions into expressions of their own identities, beliefs, and histories.

objects.title: Sandstone Garuda
objects.caption:
In the Mahabharata, an epic poem from ancient India known throughout Southesast Asia, the king of birds, Garuda, battles the gods for divine nectar (amrita), which the naga serpents have demanded in exchange for his mother’s freedom. Vishnu, impressed by Garuda’s courage, grants him immortality, and accepts his service as a faithful mount (vahana).

In this relief, which would have been positioned high on a wall, Garuda strides in triumph over the naga. Rulers of Champa built temples (now located mostly in central and southern Vietnam) dedicated to Buddhist deities, and to local incarnations of Shiva and Vishnu. The Cham people today are mostly Muslim, with communities in Cambodia and Vietnam.

objects.title: Elephant and Mahout Kendi
objects.caption:
A brown-glazed stoneware pouring vessel, shaped as an elephant with its rider, was recovered from a shipwreck off the coast of Brunei Darussalam in 1998. Crafted in the 15th–16th century at the Si Satchanalai kilns in Central Thailand, this striking object offers a vivid glimpse into Southeast Asia’s interconnected maritime world.
Elephants, symbols of wisdom, strength, and loyalty in Hindu-Buddhist traditions, were powerful cultural icons carried across the region by trade, ritual, and storytelling. As this elephant-shaped kendi travelled across seas, it became part of the vibrant networks that once linked Brunei, Thailand, and communities far beyond.
Today, this remarkable vessel stands as a reminder of our shared heritage, shaped by the movement of goods, ideas, beliefs, and the ocean itself. Through birds, animals, and objects carried by maritime exchange, Southeast Asian museums continue to illuminate stories of creativity, connection, and cultural dialogue across the region.

objects.title: Elephant Leg Bone (Elephas maximus indicus)
objects.caption:
This bone originates from the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus). Identified as a femur (posterior thigh bone), it was received by the National Museum Bangkok from the Ministry of Finance. Elephant bones such as this one served a critical industrial function in the production of Pod Duang (Bullet Money), a silver currency used from the 14th to 20th century: artisans shaped the silver by hammering it on an elephant thigh bone, preferred for its toughness and elasticity that allowed it to absorb repeated impact without deforming the metal. An example of Pod Duang (Bullet Money) appears later in this trail.

The specimen displayed here belongs to the Indian subspecies (Elephas maximus indicus), which inhabits natural forests across the Asian mainland — from Nepal, Bhutan and India through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, Malaysia, and Yunnan, China. Two further subspecies occur in the region: the Sumatran Elephant (Elephas maximus sumatranus), found only in Sumatra and generally smaller; and the Borneo Elephant (Elephas maximus borneacus), which shares a similar appearance to the Indian subspecies but carries a distinct genetic code.

Elephants are native to Southeast Asia, with elephant bones dating back to prehistoric times discovered in the region. A fossilised jaw identified as Stegodon insignis, believed to be related to modern Asian elephants and living approximately 2,000,000 to 10,000 years ago, was discovered at the headwaters of the Chao Phraya River in Thailand. Similar fossils have also been found in a limestone cave in Perak, Malaysia, and fossilised tusks in the Patiayam Mountains of Central Java, Indonesia.

Throughout history, elephants have been deeply intertwined with the way of life of Southeast Asian peoples, both symbolically and practically. They served as transport in warfare, where elephant dueling (Yuttahatthi) between opposing kings was regarded as the highest form of martial honour, and facilitated the movement of goods along trade routes through forests and mountainous terrain. A relief on the 8th-century Candi Borobudur in Indonesia depicts a Bodhisattva riding an elephant, while in the 19th century, elephants became the primary workforce in the northern Thai logging industry, especially after its expansion following Britain and France obtaining permission to open forest sawmills in Myanmar.

Elephant body parts served practical ends too. Across Maritime Southeast Asia, ivory was used for kris handles, ornaments, and furnishings, while in Thailand, elephant bone was turned on a lathe to produce walking stick handles, betel nut grinders, and boxes.The flexible and impact resistant properties of elephant bone also lent it well to forms of delicate handicrafts, such as the manufacture of the reeds of the Khaen, a traditional woodwind instrument from Northeastern Thailand and Laos.

objects.title: Elephant Molar Coconut Grater (Dwarf Elephant Bone)
objects.title_raw: Elephant Molar Coconut Grater (Dwarf Elephant Bone)
objects.collection: Folklore Museum, The Institute for Southern Thai Studies
objects.dimensions: Length: 58 cm, Width: 33 cm, Height: 18 cm
objects.object_biography: Contributed by Mrs. Sriya Kongyen, House No. 21, Ranot Sub-district, Ranot District, Songkhla Province. Data recorded on 28 January 1997. Exhibited in the Coconut Grater Room (Kratai Khud Maphrao Room), Folklore Museum, Institute of Southern Thai Studies.
objects.caption:
This coconut grater, known in Southern Thai as a lek khud maphrao, is distinguished by its base, which is fashioned from the large molar of a megafaunal animal. Attached to the front is a serrated iron blade used to shred coconut meat into fine flakes for pressing coconut milk. Elephant molars are among the densest and hardest skeletal structures in the animal kingdom, making them well suited to withstand repeated pressure and impact. The use of this material reflects local knowledge in repurposing durable natural resources for everyday life.

Elders around the Songkhla Lake Basin believe this molar belonged to the “dwarf elephant” (chang khrae or chang khom), which is said to have once inhabited the peat swamps and wetlands of Southern Thailand. Folk memory places these elephants across Songkhla Province, Nakhon Si Thammarat, and Phatthalung Province, before they vanished roughly eight decades ago. Some accounts tell of villagers spotting elephants foraging in the twilight hours or slipping into paddy fields to feed. These sightings prompted the community to band together in a regional herding cry to drive them back into the wilderness. Certain locals also compare these creatures to the pygmy elephants of Sabah, Malaysia. Though scientific evidence remains inconclusive, these oral histories and folklore preserve a community’s memory of its landscape and its long relationship with elephants.

The idea of miniature elephants also appears in classical Thai treatises on elephant lore (Kotchasat) and ancient Southern palm-leaf manuscripts (Nangshue Bod), which document unusual elephant phenotypes under names such as chang klaeb(husk-sized elephants) and chang khom (stunted elephants). Beyond folklore, elephant molars have long been regarded in Thai society as auspicious protective amulets, believed to bestow Metta Mahaniyom (loving-kindness and popularity) and ward off misfortune.

These beliefs were not confined to ritual or spiritual practice, but were also embedded in everyday life. Coconut is central to Southern Thai cuisine, and the coconut grater was an essential household tool as well as a focus of communal life during merit-making ceremonies, festivals, and weddings. Villagers often gathered to share labour in the tradition known as ok pak khud phrao (“asking for mouths to grate coconuts”). By transforming a molar attributed to the dwarf elephants of local folk memory into a tool of daily use, this coconut grater demonstrates how material culture preserves human relationships with elephants and the landscapes they once shared.

objects.title: Elephant-Shaped Relic Containers
objects.place_of_production: Wat Chedi Sung, Hod sub-district, Hod district, Chiang Mai province
objects.dimensions: Width 1.1 cm, Height 4.5 cm, Length 7 cm
objects.object_biography: Acquired from Wat Chedi Sung, Hod sub-district, Hod district, Chiang Mai province, in 1960.
objects.caption:
These miniature relic containers, fashioned from quartz and semi-precious stones, were discovered in 1960 at Wat Chedi Sung in Chiang Mai province, Thailand. They date to the Lanna period of the 16th century.
Relic containers of this type served as receptacles for Buddha’s relics, i.e., bodily fragments attributed to the historical Buddha. These relics were enshrined within a stupa or other sacred structures as objects of veneration. The animal forms chosen for such containers were not arbitrary. In fact creatures regarded as auspicious within Hindu-Buddhist traditions typically shaped these vessels to hold sacred material. Thus, the animal forms reinforced the sanctity and spiritual significance of what was held within.
The elephant form also evokes the Buddha’s previous lives as recounted in the Jataka tales, which are narratives of the Bodhisattva’s many births across human and animal forms. These tales are central to Buddhist traditions across mainland Southeast Asia. In one story, the Bodhisattva appears as an elephant king who willingly offers his tusks to a forester, thus embodying ideals of generosity and selflessness. In another, he is reborn as the king of the six-tusked elephants. Hunted because of a past grievance, the elephant king chooses not to harm the hunter upon seeing him dressed in the saffron robes of a monk, thus demonstrating compassion and restraint even in the face of suffering.
The elephant form connected these relic containers to the Buddha’s sacred presence by recalling narratives of compassion, sacrifice, and moral virtue. These narratives continued to be shared widely in Southeast Asian Buddhist traditions.

objects.title: Ganesha
objects.object_biography: The Dutch government in Java presented this to King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) of Thailand during his visit in 1896.
objects.caption:
Carved from volcanic stone, this monumental statue depicts Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity associated with wisdom, learning, and the removal of obstacles. According to Hindu tradition, Ganesha acquired his elephant head after Shiva restored him to life using the head of the first living creature encountered by his attendants. As the deity invoked at the beginning of new undertakings, he came to embody knowledge, good fortune, and successful beginnings.

The elephant's form draws on meanings that extend beyond Ganesha himself. Across South and Southeast Asia, elephants were admired for their strength, intelligence, and close relationship with water and agricultural fertility. In Hindu tradition, these qualities were also expressed through Airavata, the celestial elephant of Indra, whose association with rain and abundance reflects the importance of elephants within agrarian societies. Ganesha's rounded body likewise came to symbolise the fullness of the harvest and prosperity.

Beneath Ganesha appears his companion, the mouse. Although small, it represents the obstacles, desires, and disruptions that can hinder human life. By placing the mouse beneath him, Ganesha demonstrates his mastery over these forces, reinforcing his role as the remover of obstacles.

This sculpture reflects how communities across Southeast Asia continually reinterpreted the elephant through religious imagination and artistic practice. In the figure of Ganesha, one of the region's most familiar animals became a powerful expression of wisdom, protection, prosperity, and renewal.

objects.title: Gringsing
objects.collection: Department of Museums Malaysia (Jabatan Muzium Malaysia)
objects.caption:
Did you know that Bali’s sacred gringsing cloth and India’s exquisite patola share one of the rarest textile techniques in the world? Both are created using double ikat, a mastery practiced in only three places globally: Gujarat (India), Bali (Indonesia), and Okinawa (Japan).
From the 11th to the 19th century, Gujarati patola travelled widely across the Indian Ocean through Gujarati Muslim merchants, reaching ports in Sumatra, Malay courts, Java, Bali, and the Spice Islands Across Southeast Asia, patola became a symbol of prestige and spiritual protection.
Evidence shows that it directly influenced local weaving traditions. This shared heritage traces back to centuries of maritime trade. Gujarati patola, like the stunning piece housed at the National Museum of Malaysia, circulated among royal courts and coastal communities.
These luxurious cloths inspired new local traditions, including in Tenganan Pegringsingan in Bali, where weavers transformed the imported technique into their own spiritually potent Geringsing. Tenganan’s oral histories even recount that their ancestors once received a sacred patola from India, which became the foundation for developing their distinct patterns and ritual meanings.
Together, patola and gringsing remind us how craftsmanship, ideas, and symbols moved across the sea, weaving a shared heritage between India and Southeast Asia that continues to inspire today
